Our operations are subject to permits and consent decrees administered under the Clean Water Act and comparable state requirements, which limit discharges of pollutants and establish monitoring, reporting and maintenance obligations. There can be no assurance that our treatment systems will operate as intended during periods of heavy usage, equipment downtime, extreme weather or changes in raw material characteristics. Exceedances, even if inadvertent, may result in notices of violation, permit modifications, increased monitoring, penalties or requirement to implement costly upgrades.

Our facilities may also encounter contamination risks from historical operations, storage tanks, underground piping and third-party shipments. Contamination could migrate to surface water or groundwater, requiring remediation and potentially constraining future site use. In some cases, remediation obligations can extend for many years and may not be fully recoverable from insurance or other parties.

If we are unable to maintain compliance with wastewater permit conditions or if environmental liabilities arise from past or current discharges, our costs, operational flexibility and reputation could be materially adversely affected.

Compliance is sensitive to operating conditions, including feedstock variability, product mix, maintenance practices and the performance of pollution control equipment. The failure of control systems, inaccurate monitoring, or delays in corrective maintenance could result in emissions that exceed permit thresholds.

In addition, we can be subject to claims related to alleged off-site impacts from air emissions. Communities near our facilities may experience odor, dust or other nuisance conditions and may seek enforcement actions or litigation. Even where an exceedance is minor, regulators may require additional capital expenditures or impose restrictions on production schedules.

Regulatory standards for certain pollutants may tighten over time. New classification of hazardous air pollutants or requirements to adopt best available control technologies could increase operating expenses and capital needs. We cannot predict the timing, scope or cost of complying with future emission rules, including potential obligations to investigate legacy conditions associated with previous production activity.

risk_heading: Remediation Obligations for Hazardous Materials
paragraph_text:
We store and handle chemicals and other hazardous materials at our sites, and some of these materials have the potential to cause contamination if released. Environmental laws generally impose liability for contamination regardless of fault and may apply to current and former owners and operators. As a result, even if we are not directly responsible for legacy contamination at a property, we may be required to conduct investigations, implement interim controls or undertake remediation to satisfy regulatory requirements.

Remediation costs can be significant and depend on the nature and extent of contamination, the performance of remediation technologies, and the requirements of regulators. Cleanup timeframes can extend for years, particularly where contaminants have migrated into soils or groundwater or where multiple parties may contribute to the contamination. Regulatory oversight and community scrutiny may also increase the likelihood of delays, additional studies and changes to the remediation plan.

We may also face obligations related to underground storage tanks, historical disposal practices and waste burial activities. If environmental assessments identify previously unknown contamination, remediation scope and associated costs may increase. Any such liabilities, whether covered by insurance or indemnities, could materially affect our results of operations and cash flows.

We store and handle chemicals and other hazardous materials at our sites, and some of these materials have the potential to cause contamination if released. Environmental laws generally impose liability for contamination regardless of fault and may apply to current and former owners and operators. As a result, even if we are not directly responsible for legacy contamination at a property, we may be required to conduct investigations, implement interim controls or undertake remediation to satisfy regulatory requirements.

Remediation costs can be significant and depend on the nature and extent of contamination, the performance of remediation technologies, and the requirements of regulators. Cleanup timeframes can extend for years, particularly where contaminants have migrated into soils or groundwater or where multiple parties may contribute to the contamination. Regulatory oversight and community scrutiny may also increase the likelihood of delays, additional studies and changes to the remediation plan.

We may also face obligations related to underground storage tanks, historical disposal practices and waste burial activities. If environmental assessments identify previously unknown contamination, remediation scope and associated costs may increase. Any such liabilities, whether covered by insurance or indemnities, could materially affect our results of operations and cash flows.
label: Pollution & Waste
generation_notes: Covers remediation, hazardous materials releases, legacy contamination, regulatory liability—within Pollution & Waste.

risk_heading: Packaging Waste and Extended Producer Responsibility
paragraph_text:
We sell products that may require packaging materials such as plastics, foams, corrugated paper and protective films. Increasing regulatory and customer expectations regarding packaging waste, recyclability and recycled content could require redesigns, changes to sourcing and higher costs. Certain jurisdictions have adopted or are considering extended producer responsibility or similar regimes that require companies to finance collection, recycling and disposal of packaging waste associated with products sold into those jurisdictions.

If we fail to meet applicable reporting obligations or targets, or if recycled content requirements become stricter, we could be subject to penalties, loss of market access in certain locations, or the need to obtain third-party credits at higher cost. Product distribution changes, seasonal demand fluctuations and supply constraints may also affect our ability to procure packaging that satisfies evolving specifications.

In addition, packaging waste management may depend on the performance of recycling infrastructure. If the recycled materials produced from our packaging are not accepted by processing facilities, we could face higher waste disposal costs or be required to increase the proportion of packaging that is actually recovered.

While we monitor regulatory developments, we cannot predict the timing or impact of new requirements. Failure to adapt could adversely affect profitability.

risk_heading: Hazardous Waste Contractor and Manifest Compliance Risks
paragraph_text:
Our operations require the disposal of hazardous and non-hazardous waste streams, including solvent residues, contaminated filters, and wastewater treatment by-products. The transportation and disposal of these wastes are subject to detailed requirements, such as waste characterization, generator determinations, labeling and manifest procedures. If our internal classification processes are incomplete or if documentation provided to carriers and disposal facilities is inaccurate, regulators may allege noncompliance.

We depend on licensed third parties for treatment and disposal, and we may not control their operations, equipment uptime or compliance practices. If a waste shipment is delayed, lost or rejected by a treatment facility, we could incur additional costs for re-handling and storage and could face regulatory scrutiny. Likewise, if a contractor improperly manages waste after accepting it, we may still face enforcement actions or remediation obligations as a generator or prior owner.

Environmental enforcement can involve administrative orders, consent decrees, civil penalties and injunctive relief. The resulting expenditures could include installing additional storage capacity, increasing monitoring and training, and engaging third-party consultants.

Because waste characterization can be complex and waste streams can change based on operating conditions and product mix, we cannot ensure that our compliance programs will be sufficient to prevent violations.

risk_heading: E-Waste Collection, Processing and Disposal Risks
paragraph_text:
We refurbish and distribute certain electronic products and may be required to participate in programs that collect, recycle or dispose of end-of-life equipment. Disposal of e-waste involves regulatory requirements for data handling, storage, transport, recycling processes and appropriate treatment of components containing hazardous substances. While we implement procedures intended to meet these requirements, compliance may be affected by changes in local regulations, differences in program administration across jurisdictions, and variations in how third-party recyclers process materials.

If recycling partners do not separate hazardous components properly, fail to meet throughput and documentation requirements, or improperly export materials, regulators may investigate and seek penalties. In addition, any failure in our own data erasure and handling procedures could increase the risk of privacy and public claims, which may lead to additional remediation and compliance costs.

E-waste programs may also impose fees or require financial commitments based on volumes collected. Reduced participation rates in a given region, or shifts in the composition of end-of-life products we receive, could increase the cost per unit processed.

If we are unable to manage our e-waste obligations in a compliant and cost-effective manner, our operating costs could increase and our relationships with customers and program administrators could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Spill and Release Risks During Transportation and Storage
paragraph_text:
We use and transport materials that can be harmful to human health or the environment, including intermediate chemicals and solvents. These materials may be shipped by rail, truck or vessel and stored in tanks, drums and bulk containers at our facilities. Our operations are subject to safety and environmental requirements governing storage integrity, secondary containment, loading and unloading procedures and emergency preparedness. Accidents, including vehicle collisions, equipment failures, or human error, could result in spills or releases.

Any spill could require immediate containment and cleanup, suspension of operations, notification obligations and engagement with federal and state agencies. Even releases that do not cause immediate regulatory violations may generate cleanup liabilities and long-term remediation obligations if contaminants migrate to soil or groundwater. Insurance may not cover the full amount of claims, including costs related to regulatory oversight, lost production, or consequential damages.

In addition, certain transportation routes may be constrained by restrictions or shifting enforcement priorities, which could affect logistics and increase the risk of handling incidents. We cannot assure that our training, procedures and monitoring will prevent all releases.

Because spills may occur infrequently but with potentially large consequences, we may incur costs and liabilities that could materially adversely affect our business.

risk_heading: Industrial By-Product Recycling and Market Acceptance Risks
paragraph_text:
We generate industrial by-products that may be suitable for recycling, re-use or beneficial use depending on regulatory classifications and customer demand. While we seek to minimize waste sent to landfills by directing certain streams to recycling arrangements, the ability to classify by-products as non-hazardous secondary materials and the economic feasibility of recycling may change. Regulators may require additional testing, impose restrictions on use, or reclassify certain materials if they find that they pose greater environmental risks.

Recycling markets for recovered materials can also be volatile. If the demand for recycled feedstock declines, processing facilities reduce capacity, or contamination levels increase, we may be required to treat by-products as waste and dispose of them at higher cost. Quality requirements for recycled inputs can be stringent, and changes in production technology or upstream materials may affect the consistency of by-products.

In some cases, our recycling partners rely on equipment and permitting status that we do not control. If a partner’s permits lapse or if a partner discontinues a recycling line, we may need to identify alternative recyclers quickly, increasing costs and operational disruption.

Our failure to maintain beneficial-use pathways for by-products could increase waste disposal costs and increase exposure to environmental liabilities.

risk_heading: Mine Tailings and Solid Waste Management Risks
paragraph_text:
Where we operate extraction-related activities, we create solid waste and residual materials that must be stored and managed to prevent releases of contaminants. Tailings and waste rock piles, settling ponds and related infrastructure are subject to engineering, design and monitoring standards, as well as periodic inspections by regulatory authorities. Changes in rainfall patterns, unexpected geotechnical conditions, equipment malfunctions, or operating deviations can increase the risk of dam integrity issues or overflow events.

Any release of tailings or leachate could impact nearby surface waters and require extensive cleanup, including capture systems, water treatment and long-term monitoring. Regulators may impose additional constraints on production, require modifications to tailings management practices and demand updated closure plans.

Closure and post-closure obligations can be expensive and depend on the final condition of the waste structures. Even after operations cease, we may remain responsible for maintaining controls and addressing seepage or erosion concerns. We may also be exposed to third-party claims alleging property damage or personal injury related to alleged contamination.

We maintain controls and monitoring programs, but there can be no assurance that these measures will prevent all environmental incidents or that future regulatory requirements will not increase the cost of solid waste management.

If we experience a significant chemical release or fail to respond adequately, our costs and potential liabilities could be material.

risk_heading: Legacy Site Liabilities Following Asset Sales
paragraph_text:
From time to time, we acquire or sell assets and may assume or retain environmental responsibilities under contractual arrangements. Even where a sale agreement provides for indemnification, recovery from other parties may be limited by their financial condition, insurance availability or the scope of indemnity. Environmental laws can also impose direct liability on current owners and operators based on ownership, control or historic disposal activity, regardless of contractual allocation.

When sites are transferred, we conduct assessments intended to identify recognized environmental conditions. However, assessments may not identify all contamination and may not detect issues that arise from unknown or undisclosed historical releases. In addition, contamination can migrate over time. If new information becomes available or if regulators require additional investigation or cleanup, we could incur expenses that exceed our reserves.

We may also be required to provide ongoing access for sampling, monitor treatment systems and maintain institutional controls, such as restrictions on groundwater use. Such obligations can affect potential redevelopment timelines and reduce the value of certain assets.

While we attempt to manage these risks through due diligence and contractual protections, we cannot assure that we will not incur material costs related to legacy pollution or waste disposal activities.

risk_heading: Solid Waste Disposal Constraints and Landfill Closure Costs
paragraph_text:
We generate waste from manufacturing and maintenance activities, including contaminated rags, spent catalysts, filter media and non-hazardous industrial waste. Disposal practices depend on permitted landfill capacity and the availability of waste treatment facilities. If landfills near our operations reach capacity, if permits are revoked, or if regulations require stricter waste segregation and treatment, our disposal options may narrow.

Higher disposal costs and transportation expenses may result if we must ship waste longer distances to alternative facilities. In addition, landfill closure, post-closure care and remediation obligations may be funded through per-ton fees or other assessments imposed on waste generators and operators. Changes in these assessments could increase costs unexpectedly.

Some wastes may also be subject to more restrictive classifications over time, including reclassification of materials as hazardous. Such reclassifications could require different handling, storage and disposal methods, further increasing costs and operational complexity.

We attempt to reduce waste generation and improve recycling rates; however, not all waste streams can be recycled profitably or consistently. If we cannot secure disposal services at manageable cost or if we face new disposal restrictions, our operating margins could be negatively impacted.

If actual remediation costs are higher than estimated or if liability is expanded due to new regulatory requirements or discovery of additional contamination, our costs could increase and our cash flows could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Refrigerant Leaks and Ongoing Waste Handling for Closed Systems
paragraph_text:
Some of our facilities use refrigerants and other chemicals in closed systems for cooling and process equipment. Although these systems are designed to be leak-resistant, they require periodic maintenance, servicing and eventual decommissioning. Handling and disposing of refrigerants and other materials are subject to environmental regulations regarding containment, recovery, and proper treatment to prevent releases to air and improper disposal as waste.

If technicians fail to contain refrigerants during servicing or if seals deteriorate unexpectedly, releases could occur and trigger regulatory reporting obligations, penalties and the need to implement additional engineering controls. Decommissioning older equipment may also generate waste materials such as contaminated components, insulating materials and service residues, which may require specialized disposal routes.

We rely on third-party contractors for certain service activities, including recovery, transportation and disposal. Contractor noncompliance or incomplete documentation could create liability for us. In addition, refrigerant availability and pricing can change quickly depending on regulatory and market conditions, which may affect service costs and lead times.

While we seek to operate these systems responsibly, we cannot guarantee that releases, improper handling or disposal failures will not occur. Any such events could result in increased operating expenses and potential enforcement or litigation risk.

risk_heading: Changes to Hazardous Waste Definitions and Treatment Standards

These determinations depend on chemical composition, concentration and other factors, and regulators may revise definitions and testing methods. As we process new product lines or source materials from different suppliers, the waste characteristics generated by our operations may shift, potentially resulting in different hazard classifications.

If certain waste streams become newly classified as hazardous or if existing classifications are challenged by regulators, we would need to implement additional segregation, labeling, storage controls and permitted disposal pathways. These changes could increase compliance costs and require capital expenditures for new handling equipment or storage capacity.

In addition, treatment standards for hazardous waste—such as permitted incineration conditions, stabilization requirements and landfill acceptance criteria—may tighten over time. Even when we are compliant today, we cannot assure we will remain in compliance with future standards.

We seek to manage these risks through waste characterization testing and supplier controls. However, testing programs may involve sampling limitations and cannot guarantee that waste streams will consistently meet assumptions throughout operating cycles.

Any increase in the costs of waste classification, treatment or disposal could adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition.

Local ordinances and state air permits may require controls such as water spraying, covered trucks, stabilized entrances, emission monitoring and operational restrictions during certain weather conditions. Regulators may impose corrective actions, require additional controls, or issue fines for fugitive emissions. risk_heading: Discharge Permitting, Wastewater Treatment, and Waterway Contamination Risk
paragraph_text:
We discharge treated wastewater and other industrial water streams from certain operations pursuant to permits issued under federal, state and local requirements. Permit conditions typically limit concentrations and total volumes of pollutants, require specific monitoring and reporting, and mandate operational controls for treatment systems. If our wastewater treatment processes are disrupted, insufficiently staffed, improperly maintained or impacted by abnormal process conditions, discharges could exceed permit limits or include constituents not anticipated in our designs.

Even where discharges do not result in immediate notice or regulatory action, releases may contribute to contamination of nearby waterways, groundwater or stormwater systems, which could trigger investigations, enforcement actions and remediation obligations. Some contaminants associated with our operations can persist and migrate, increasing the duration and scope of potential remediation. Moreover, third-party contractors that handle sampling, laboratory analysis or maintenance may contribute to reporting errors or nonconforming performance.

Costs to address noncompliance or contamination—such as filtration upgrades, chemical treatment optimization, additional monitoring, and long-term remediation—could be material and could adversely affect our financial condition.

risk_heading: Emissions of Toxic Substances and Air Permit Enforcement
paragraph_text:
Certain facilities are subject to air emissions permits and operating limits for pollutants, including volatile organic compounds, particulate matter and hazardous air pollutants. While we invest in abatement systems such as scrubbers, filters and process controls, emissions can vary due to equipment wear, changes in raw materials, maintenance upsets, startup and shutdown conditions, and extreme weather that affects operating parameters. Any failure to operate within permit limits may result in exceedances, emissions events and associated costs.

Regulators can impose penalties, require additional monitoring, mandate corrective action plans, or restrict operations while compliance issues are addressed. Private parties may also assert claims related to alleged property damage or personal injury arising from emissions. In addition, air permit requirements can change as agencies update air quality standards and revise interpretations of existing regulations, which may require us to incur capital expenditures to upgrade control technologies.

If we experience repeated noncompliance or a significant emissions incident, we could face materially higher operating costs, increased legal expense, and reputational harm. These impacts could adversely affect results of operations, cash flows and access to financing.

risk_heading: Contamination from Historical Operations and Remediation Obligations
paragraph_text:
Some properties we occupy or have used in prior periods may contain or have contained hazardous substances, petroleum products or other pollutants from past industrial activities conducted by us or by predecessor or third parties. Although we perform environmental assessments and maintain remediation plans where required, contamination discovered during development, redevelopment or routine maintenance could be more extensive than expected. Conditions may also be obscured by soil depth, underground utilities, or changes in site hydrology that complicate identification and containment.

Environmental remediation obligations can include investigation, excavation and disposal of contaminated materials, treatment of groundwater, installation of monitoring wells, and long-term maintenance. These obligations may be imposed by regulators or by other potentially responsible parties, and the allocation of liability among parties is often uncertain. Even if contamination results from activities not directly attributable to us, we may still be responsible as a current operator.

In addition, remediation techniques may require continuous effectiveness monitoring and can be ineffective if conditions change, such as during flooding or changes to water tables. Any significant remediation event could require substantial cash outlays, impact production schedules and increase liability exposure.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Transporting Hazardous and Regulated Waste
paragraph_text:
We rely on third-party carriers and disposal facilities to transport and process certain hazardous and regulated wastes generated in our operations. These wastes may include chemical residues, contaminated rags and filters, spent catalysts, and materials classified under multiple regulatory categories. The movement of these materials involves risks of spills, leaks, improper labeling, loss of custody, and container damage during loading or transit.

If a release occurs, we could be required to remediate affected areas and respond to regulator inquiries, even if the incident is attributable to the carrier or the receiving facility. Furthermore, regulators may scrutinize our waste characterization, manifests, and documentation practices; errors in classification or tracking could be treated as noncompliance. In some instances, disposal facilities can reject materials based on acceptability criteria, causing delays and requiring alternative disposal arrangements, which may increase costs.

Our ability to manage these risks depends on the performance of counterparties and the accuracy of our waste profiling. Counterparty disruptions, labor shortages, or changes in disposal site availability could increase transportation distances and handling steps, raising the likelihood of incidents and the cost of compliance.

risk_heading: Packaging and Product Waste Management and Recycling Program Compliance

We produce products that require packaging and protective materials for shipment to customers and downstream distributors. Compliance with evolving packaging and recycling requirements—such as extended producer responsibility laws, takeback mandates, and material labeling rules—can require changes to packaging composition, documentation, and recycling arrangements. Failure to meet these obligations could result in fines, injunctive relief, and increased costs to retrofit packaging or remediate noncompliant inventory.

We also distribute products that may generate waste at end of life, including filters and components that may contain regulated substances. While we work to reduce hazardous content and to coordinate with authorized recyclers, the overall effectiveness of recycling depends on consumer participation, collection infrastructure, and the quality of downstream processing. If recyclers fail to properly manage materials, or if we are unable to source sufficient recycling capacity meeting regulatory criteria, we could face compliance gaps.

In certain jurisdictions, verification and reporting requirements for recycling performance may be strict and subject to audit. Material inaccuracies in reported volumes or failure to demonstrate compliance could trigger penalties and reputational damage.

risk_heading: Hazardous Material Spills and Emergency Response Costs
paragraph_text:
We store chemicals, fuels and industrial materials at our facilities. Accidental releases can occur as a result of equipment malfunctions, human error, corrosion, extreme temperatures, natural disasters, or transportation activities within the site. Even with safety controls and emergency response plans, releases of hazardous materials can lead to environmental contamination, employee exposure concerns, and interruptions to operations.

If a spill reaches soil or stormwater systems, it may contaminate surrounding properties and require extensive sampling, containment, and cleanup. Regulators can require immediate notification, impose investigation obligations, and require modifications to storage practices, engineering controls and monitoring. Additionally, third parties may bring claims related to bodily injury, property damage, or diminution of land value.

Emergency remediation can require specialized contractors and can occur on accelerated timelines, increasing costs. Insurance may not cover all expenses or may be subject to deductibles and coverage limits. Where contamination is severe, cleanup may extend beyond one reporting period and could adversely affect cash flows and results of operations.

risk_heading: E-Waste Disposal and Data Center Equipment Takeback Risks

In addition, certain jurisdictions require producers or service providers to finance takeback programs or meet collection and recycling targets. Meeting these obligations may require contracts with certified recyclers and tracking of material flows. Disruptions in recycler capacity, changes in certification standards, or limitations on shipment routes can delay recycling and increase storage costs at our sites.

We also must ensure that equipment destruction and refurbishing practices follow applicable requirements for secure handling. While information security is managed separately, failure to coordinate destruction processes with environmental compliance could expose us to regulatory scrutiny.

Any failure to manage e-waste and related obligations could lead to penalties, cost overruns and damage to customer and regulator relationships.

We may also be required to revise packaging and containment specifications to reduce the likelihood or severity of releases, which could increase operating expenses.

risk_heading: Regulatory Changes Affecting Hazardous Waste Classification and Disposal Costs
paragraph_text:
From time to time, environmental agencies update regulations and guidance that affect how wastes are classified and treated. Such changes can alter whether certain process residues are deemed hazardous, whether recycling qualifies for regulatory exemptions, and what documentation is required for transport and disposal. Because our production involves multiple material streams, the classification of specific residues can depend on sampling results, variability in inputs and test methods.

If regulators interpret existing rules differently, we could be required to re-characterize materials currently handled under lower regulatory burdens. That could increase the frequency and cost of hazardous waste treatment and disposal, extend storage and handling requirements, and require additional permitting for storage containers and accumulation areas. Noncompliance with new or revised requirements may also result in enforcement actions, permit modifications, and civil penalties.

Additionally, third-party disposal providers may change their acceptability requirements or discontinue receiving certain wastes, which could require us to identify alternative vendors and incur higher transportation and disposal costs.

The resulting cost increases, operational disruptions, and potential liabilities could be material.

risk_heading: Product Manufacturing Residues and Solvent Use Leading to Toxic Release Risks
paragraph_text:
We use chemical processes that generate residues and spent solvents that must be captured, treated and disposed of in accordance with applicable environmental requirements. Our operations depend on the performance of containment systems, ventilation, solvent recovery equipment and related monitoring to prevent releases to air and to the environment. If those systems fail or perform below expected levels—due to maintenance gaps, incorrect operating parameters, or unanticipated reactions—residues could escape containment.

In certain cases, solvent-related releases can result in odors, visible emissions or emissions of regulated air pollutants. They may also increase the burden on wastewater systems if contaminated streams are routed improperly. Remediation may include vapor mitigation, soil testing and cleanup, and replacement of activated carbon or other treatment media.

We may also be required to conduct long-term monitoring where volatile compounds migrate or where contamination is detected in surrounding areas. Contractual and regulatory obligations may require us to demonstrate that capture efficiencies and treatment effectiveness meet specified thresholds.

Any significant release or inability to demonstrate compliance could lead to enforcement actions, increased insurance premiums, and higher remediation and operating costs.

If runoff contains pollutants above permitted limits, we could face enforcement actions under stormwater permitting programs. Regulators may also increase monitoring requirements or impose additional operational limitations during certain weather conditions.

Private parties may claim that pollutants impacted nearby properties or water resources. Further, failure to maintain accurate records of inspections, sampling results and corrective actions can be treated as noncompliance.

Any material stormwater incident or regulatory outcome could adversely affect our operating costs and could lead to remediation obligations.

Any failure to manage sludge and by-product disposal in compliance with applicable requirements could result in penalties, remediation costs and business disruptions.

risk_heading: Contamination Risks in Chemical Manufacturing and Mixing Operations
paragraph_text:
Our chemical and materials processing operations involve mixing, heating and transfer of compounds that can produce by-products and waste streams requiring treatment. Contamination can occur when equipment is not cleaned adequately between batches, when seals and gaskets fail, or when mislabeling leads to incorrect material transfers. Even minor contamination can change the characteristics of waste streams, including pH, chemical reactivity and concentrations of regulated constituents.

If contaminated waste is not identified before disposal, it may be rejected by treatment or landfill facilities or may require higher-cost hazardous handling. Mischaracterized wastes can also increase the likelihood of regulatory enforcement if regulators determine that our reporting and sampling practices were inadequate.

Cleaning and changeover activities can introduce additional waste in the form of rinses, spent cleaning solutions and absorbents. If these wastes are not properly collected and treated, they may contribute to environmental releases.

We use quality controls and training to reduce these risks; however, process control relies on consistent adherence to procedures and equipment performance. Any event resulting in a significant contamination release could result in remediation expenses, regulatory penalties, and production delays.

risk_heading: Waste Storage Permitting and Capacity Constraints
paragraph_text:
Our operations require temporary storage of waste materials pending treatment or disposal. These storage activities are subject to permit limits on volumes, container types, and accumulation times. If we experience unexpected production downtime, delays in disposal vendor schedules, or transportation constraints, waste generated during normal operations may accumulate beyond permitted capacity or accumulation time limits.

Exceeding these limits may be treated as noncompliance and can lead to enforcement actions, required corrective measures, and increased monitoring. Even when excess accumulation is temporary, regulators may require documentation of corrective actions and may require additional engineered controls such as larger containment systems or additional storage buildings, which would require capital expenditures.

Capacity constraints could also increase the risk of container handling incidents, leaks, and releases due to more frequent moves and increased storage density. Additionally, if we store wastes longer than planned, degradation of certain materials may increase the concentration of regulated constituents, complicating treatment and disposal.

While we maintain planning procedures and multiple vendor relationships, supply chain disruptions can still produce shortages in treatment capacity. Any significant interruption could result in higher costs and potential liability.

risk_heading: Potential Costs from Spill Incidents During Transportation and Storage

Many environmental regulations require prompt notification and investigation, and regulators may require ongoing remediation, sampling and documentation. Spill incidents can also trigger remediation obligations at disposal or staging areas and may affect permits for storage and handling. Even when the volume released is limited, contamination can spread if clean-up is delayed or if weather conditions accelerate migration. Insurance may not cover all losses, including regulatory penalties, downtime costs, reputational harm that affects customer relationships, and third-party claims. We may also incur costs to implement corrective actions to prevent recurrence, including additional training, changes to handling procedures and upgraded storage infrastructure. Any significant spill or repeated minor incidents could have a material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations.

risk_heading: Risks of Lead, Mercury and Other Regulated Constituents in Waste Streams

In addition, hazardous waste handling requires compliance with more stringent manifesting, packaging and storage requirements, increasing the risk of procedural errors. If our sampling protocols do not capture variability, we could misclassify waste and face enforcement actions or forced re-disposal costs. We also may incur costs to remediate contamination if metals or other constituents migrate from storage areas into soil or groundwater. Any such occurrences could materially increase our operating expenses and reduce profitability.

risk_heading: Risks Related to By-Product Handling in Chemical Manufacturing

If these materials are not properly characterized, we may transport and store them incorrectly, increasing the risk of environmental releases or regulatory noncompliance. Additionally, storage containers may require periodic inspection and maintenance to prevent corrosion, pressure relief events or leakage. If leaks occur, we could face obligations to remediate affected soils and groundwater, and to monitor nearby receptors. We may also be required to implement additional control technologies to reduce emissions associated with handling volatile by-products. Contractual disputes with waste transporters or recyclers could delay disposal or recycling, leading to temporary storage that increases risk of spills. Any of these issues could result in penalties, increased disposal and remediation costs, and interruptions in production.

risk_heading: Risks from Changes in Recycling Markets and Material Recovery Targets

Further, changes in specifications for recycled feedstocks—such as impurity thresholds or composition requirements—could render some of our waste streams less usable. Regulatory bodies in certain jurisdictions may also impose material recovery or reporting targets that could affect the cost of compliance and may require us to participate in approved programs. If we cannot meet these requirements, regulators may seek penalties or require corrective actions. In addition, if recycling partners mishandle materials, residual contaminants could be released or improperly disposed of, potentially leading to third-party claims and remediation obligations. Any disruption in recycling performance or increased waste disposal costs could adversely impact our profitability.

risk_heading: Risks Associated With Stormwater, Wastewater, and Discharge Permits
paragraph_text:
We operate facilities subject to permits and reporting requirements governing wastewater discharges, stormwater runoff, and related water pollution controls. These requirements may include limits on chemical oxygen demand, nutrients, heavy metals, pH, temperature, and other constituents, as well as monitoring, sampling, and recordkeeping obligations. Our treatment systems and internal controls are designed to comply with permit conditions; however, changes in influent quality, equipment downtime, power interruptions, extreme weather, or operational upsets can result in exceedances of permit limits or unpermitted releases.

When discharge events occur, we may be required to implement corrective actions, conduct additional monitoring, and suspend or limit operations until compliance is restored. Authorities may also impose penalties or require modifications to treatment processes that increase capital expenditures and operating costs. Moreover, certain discharges can lead to third-party claims, including allegations of property damage or health impacts for nearby landowners and communities.

Because the timing and severity of rainfall events and influent variability are difficult to forecast, our ability to maintain compliance consistently may be challenged in future periods. Any failure to comply with discharge requirements or any resulting remediation obligations could be material.

Identifying the presence, extent, and source of contamination can be complex and may require intrusive investigation, sampling, and modeling. Remediation methods may involve excavation, soil and groundwater treatment, long-term monitoring, and institutional controls. If we are required to remediate a site on an accelerated basis or if new information indicates higher contamination levels than anticipated, our financial results could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Risks of Air Emissions, Dust, and Hazardous Pollutants
paragraph_text:
Our operations and logistics activities may emit air pollutants, including particulate matter, volatile organic compounds, and other regulated hazardous air pollutants, as well as odors and fugitive emissions from equipment. We maintain controls such as filtration systems, covers, and maintenance programs intended to reduce emissions, and we operate under permits that include emissions limits and inspection obligations. Nonetheless, emissions can increase during startups and shutdowns, maintenance outages, or process upsets, and certain emissions control equipment may fail or perform below design specifications.

Regulatory agencies may tighten emissions standards, expand enforcement of nuisance odor and fugitive emissions, or revise permitting requirements, which could require additional capital expenditures and operating changes. In addition, citizen groups and neighboring facilities may submit complaints or seek injunctive relief if they believe our operations are causing harm. If an enforcement action or lawsuit results in penalties or mandated operational restrictions, our production schedule and cost structure could be impacted.

Because air dispersion conditions vary with local weather patterns and operating conditions, predicting compliance outcomes at all times may be difficult. Any significant deviation from permit limits, release of hazardous pollutants, or failure of emission controls could result in substantial liability and reputational harm.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Chemical Storage, Spills, and Release Response
paragraph_text:
We store and use chemicals in manufacturing and research activities, including substances regulated as hazardous under environmental, transportation, and workplace safety laws. Chemical storage and transfer involve inherent risks, including line leaks, valve failures, overfills, mixing errors, and incorrect segregation of incompatible materials. Although we maintain spill prevention and countermeasure plans and conduct employee training, incidents can still occur due to human error, equipment malfunction, or unforeseen operating conditions.

In the event of a spill or uncontrolled release, we could be required to contain and clean up affected areas, notify regulators and potentially impacted neighbors, and investigate the cause and extent of contamination. Cleanup costs can escalate quickly due to the need for specialized contractors, sampling, and extended monitoring. Furthermore, releases may migrate to soil or groundwater, increasing the scope and duration of remediation.

Regulatory authorities may also require additional controls or impose fines for noncompliance with release reporting requirements, permit conditions, or storage standards. Insurance may not fully cover liabilities associated with environmental contamination, particularly where policy exclusions apply or where claims exceed policy limits.

Any spill, release, or resulting remediation could adversely affect our operations and financial condition.

risk_heading: Contractor Performance and Hazardous Waste Transportation Risks
paragraph_text:
We rely on third-party contractors for waste transportation, recycling processing, and disposal services. These contractors handle hazardous and non-hazardous wastes generated by our operations, and they operate under transportation and environmental compliance requirements. Our oversight includes selection, audits, and review of manifests and confirmations; however, waste management is largely dependent on contractor practices and accuracy. Errors such as incorrect labeling, incomplete documentation, missed pickup schedules, or improper segregation of waste streams could result in regulatory violations.

Even where a manifest is issued, regulatory authorities may identify discrepancies after-the-fact, including differences between the waste described and the waste actually transported or processed. If regulators determine that waste was mishandled, we could face enforcement actions, demands to participate in cleanup, and costs associated with investigating and remediating impacts. Additionally, contract terms may limit our ability to fully recover costs, and contractors may face financial or operational constraints that affect their performance.

Transportation accidents involving hazardous materials also pose risk, including roadway incidents and improper securing of containers. A significant transportation-related release could trigger immediate response, permit and reporting obligations, and potential claims.

Any failure in hazardous waste transportation or disposal arrangements could materially harm our operations and financial condition.

risk_heading: Risks From Product Waste, Returns, and Defective Inventory Disposal
paragraph_text:

While we have procedures for returns processing, the condition of returned goods may vary and could lead to improper classification of waste or inadequate segregation of hazardous components, such as batteries, residues, or contaminated packaging.

In addition, evolving consumer return volumes, seasonal promotional activity, and supply chain disruptions can increase the volume of returned merchandise. Greater volumes can strain internal processing capacity and increase the likelihood of documentation gaps and mistakes. When returns processing results in noncompliant waste streams or accidental release of contaminants, we could face regulatory actions, remediation requirements, and increased disposal and logistics costs.

We also maintain electronics and battery-containing equipment used in operations, which becomes subject to hazardous e-waste and battery disposal rules as components reach end-of-life. Failure to comply with e-waste take-back and disposal requirements could result in penalties and mandated corrective measures.

Any significant noncompliance in disposal of returns and defective inventory could adversely affect our financial performance and reputation.

risk_heading: Risks of Nonconforming Industrial Discharges at High-Throughput Sites
paragraph_text:
Some of our facilities operate with high throughput and complex process flows, which can increase the chance of nonconforming industrial discharges. Wastewater generated during manufacturing may contain mixtures of salts, organic compounds, and suspended solids, requiring treatment and filtration. If treatment equipment becomes fouled, if chemical dosing is incorrect, or if sensors provide inaccurate readings, treated effluent may not meet permit standards. Additionally, temporary process changes—such as switching raw material batches or responding to demand—can alter effluent characteristics.

We periodically test effluent and perform compliance sampling; however, testing is subject to sampling timing, analytical variability, and potential errors. A sampling error could delay identification of noncompliance and increase the likelihood of further permit exceedances before corrective actions are taken. Regulators may also interpret monitoring requirements strictly, including requirements for sampling methods, chain-of-custody documentation, and record retention.

Where exceedances occur, we may be required to submit corrective action plans, fund enhanced treatment systems, and potentially pay penalties. In severe cases, discharges can contribute to environmental degradation and trigger third-party litigation. The resulting remediation and legal expenses could be significant.

Given the operational complexity of these sites, we cannot assure that future discharge events will not occur or that our remediation costs will not be material.

risk_heading: Evolving Standards for Wastewater Sludge and Residuals
paragraph_text:
During wastewater treatment, we generate sludge and other residuals that can be regulated depending on their composition and concentration of constituents. Disposal of sludge may require landfilling, incineration, or beneficial reuse under narrowly defined conditions. Compliance depends on accurately characterizing residuals, maintaining appropriate storage conditions, and using permitted disposal or recycling facilities.

Regulatory authorities periodically update guidance and requirements for sludge classification and handling, including restrictions on land application and tighter limits for certain contaminants. If updated standards classify our residuals more strictly, we may be required to change disposal routes, increase frequency of laboratory testing, or install additional treatment to reduce contaminant concentrations. These changes could increase operating costs and require capital investment.

We also face risks associated with residuals transport. If residuals are mislabeled, not stabilized as required, or transported in containers that do not meet specifications, we could face enforcement actions and cleanup obligations. Even in the absence of a release, disputes with disposal facilities regarding residuals acceptance criteria can cause delays and increase inventory storage.

While we maintain programs to monitor residuals quality, the chemical composition of inflows can vary across product lines and seasons. As a result, classification outcomes and compliance requirements may be more costly than currently estimated.

Any inability to manage sludge and residuals in compliance with applicable rules could materially affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Waste Minimization and Recycling Program Risks
paragraph_text:
We have implemented waste minimization and recycling initiatives intended to reduce disposal costs and meet evolving sustainability expectations. These programs depend on accurate sorting, contamination-free material streams, and reliable recycling markets. If recyclable materials are contaminated with non-recyclable content, or if sorting procedures are insufficient, facilities may reject shipments, requiring us to dispose of materials as waste rather than recycle them. Rejected shipments can result in unanticipated disposal costs and increased landfilling.

Recycling market conditions can also deteriorate due to changes in commodity pricing, shipping availability, and regulatory requirements imposed on recyclers. If recyclers reduce capacity or increase fees, we may be forced to find alternative processors, which can increase costs and create logistic challenges. Additionally, if we make forward commitments to recycling volumes that are not achieved due to production variability, we may be subject to contract penalties.

Our programs also rely on vendor compliance and accurate documentation to support recycling and waste reporting. Incomplete or inaccurate records could lead to regulatory issues and disputes regarding whether materials were properly recycled or disposed.

Because waste generation is tied to manufacturing throughput and product mix, we cannot assure that our recycling rates will remain stable. Any failure to meet waste management objectives or to comply with reporting requirements could negatively affect our operating results and cash flows.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Hazardous Materials Transport and Storage During Projects
paragraph_text:
From time to time, we undertake construction and maintenance projects that require temporary storage and transport of hazardous materials, such as industrial lubricants, cleaning agents, and specialty coatings. During these projects, materials may be staged in temporary containers near active work areas, creating risks associated with improper storage height, deteriorating container seals, and unrecognized compatibility issues between chemicals. While we maintain safety procedures and require contractors to follow environmental requirements, we may still experience noncompliance due to scheduling pressures or inadequate contractor oversight.

If any temporary storage area is found noncompliant, or if hazardous materials are released into drainage systems through storms, we may be required to conduct rapid cleanup, submit notices, and implement additional containment controls. In certain situations, authorities can interpret storm-related transport of contaminants as an environmental violation even when the release is accidental.

We also must ensure that waste generated during projects, including spent absorbents, contaminated PPE, and removed coatings, is properly characterized and disposed. Misclassification of these wastes can lead to incorrect disposal routes and increased enforcement exposure. In addition, project delays can extend the period during which hazardous materials are stored on-site.

Any failure to manage hazardous materials and construction-related waste in compliance with applicable requirements could result in fines, remediation costs, and operational disruptions.

risk_heading: Risks From Effluent Treatment Upsets and Chemical Overdosing
paragraph_text:
Our effluent treatment operations rely on chemical dosing and process control systems to remove contaminants and meet discharge limits. These systems can be impacted by mechanical failures, sensor drift, incorrect calibration, and changes in incoming water chemistry. In some cases, power fluctuations or software errors may disrupt automated dosing schedules. If dosing is insufficient, contaminants may pass through treatment. If dosing is excessive, treated effluent may create new compliance issues, such as increased dissolved solids or pH excursions, and can affect sludge generation and disposal.

While we employ preventive maintenance, calibration procedures, and operator training, complex processes increase the risk of human error and the likelihood that issues may not be detected quickly. Sampling and reporting schedules also create a time lag between an upset event and confirmation that permit limits have been exceeded.

Permit conditions may require immediate reporting of certain events, and failure to report could result in additional penalties. Additionally, repeated upsets could lead regulators to require expanded monitoring, impose stricter limits, or require capital improvements to redundant equipment.

If we experience material treatment upsets or noncompliant discharges, we may face enforcement actions, third-party claims, and remediation obligations that could adversely affect our financial condition.

risk_heading: E-Waste Disposal and Information Technology Retention Risks
paragraph_text:
We manage information technology and industrial control equipment that becomes obsolete over time. Disposal of electronic equipment may be subject to hazardous waste rules and, in certain jurisdictions, e-waste take-back requirements. Our retirement and disposal processes are intended to ensure that computers, servers, sensors, and related components are handled by permitted recyclers and that hazardous constituents are not improperly discarded.

However, if retired equipment is stored longer than required, damaged during transfer, or partially dismantled without proper procedures, we could generate regulated waste streams or inadvertently create improper disposal paths. In addition, where equipment disposal involves returning devices to vendors or resellers, we rely on their processes and documentation for chain-of-custody and recycling confirmation. Any failure by a third party to process equipment in compliance with applicable requirements could expose us to regulatory scrutiny.

We also face risk that data destruction procedures may be inadequate. Although cybersecurity is not the primary focus of this risk, improper handling of disposed hardware could increase compliance challenges in investigations related to records retention and waste processing.

If we are unable to demonstrate compliance with e-waste requirements or if regulators identify improper disposal or incomplete documentation, we could incur penalties, be required to retrieve and reprocess material, and incur additional disposal costs.

risk_heading: Water Contamination Risk From Industrial Cleaning and Washout Activities

Industrial cleaning of equipment and facilities can generate wastewaters containing detergents, oils, and potentially regulated contaminants. We conduct cleaning through washout areas and retention systems designed to capture and treat waste streams. Nevertheless, cleaning activities can create risks if washout containment systems overflow, if hoses or connections leak, or if cleaning chemicals are used outside prescribed parameters. Weather events may also affect drainage and increase the chance of washwater reaching storm drains.

If wastewaters are not fully captured and treated, contaminated water could enter onsite drainage networks or nearby waterways, triggering regulatory reporting obligations and remediation. Even where a release is small, regulators may require investigation and sampling to determine whether environmental harm occurred.

We maintain training and standard operating procedures, including checklists and inspection requirements, but the effectiveness of these measures may be reduced during periods of staffing changes, increased workload, or contract labor usage. Additionally, if downstream treatment capacity becomes constrained, cleaning waste may require hold-and-treat scheduling that can delay operations and lead to temporary storage.

A failure to control cleaning-related discharges and washout activities could result in enforcement actions, third-party claims, and increased compliance costs that could be material to our operating results.

risk_heading: Regulatory Enforcement Risk for Hazardous Waste Classification and Manifests
paragraph_text:
Environmental compliance requires accurate hazardous waste classification and complete tracking of wastes through generators, transporters, and disposal facilities. Our compliance program includes waste sampling, laboratory analysis, and maintenance of waste manifests and records. However, waste characterization can be complex where waste contains mixtures of materials, and analytical results can vary due to sampling methods, holding times, and laboratory variability. In addition, changes in raw materials, formulations, or process conditions can alter the hazardous characteristics of waste streams.

If we misclassify a waste stream, use an incorrect waste code, or provide incomplete or incorrect manifest information, regulators may pursue enforcement actions even if the waste was ultimately disposed of appropriately. Authorities may also require us to correct records retroactively, conduct additional testing, and provide new documentation to demonstrate compliance. Violations can trigger penalties, additional reporting requirements, and, in certain circumstances, obligations to fund third-party response actions.

Furthermore, our ability to maintain compliant documentation depends on timely receipt of confirmations from transporters and disposal facilities. Disputes between counterparties about waste descriptions or delays in confirmations can increase the risk of incomplete closure of manifests.

We cannot assure that our classification, sampling, and recordkeeping practices will always withstand regulatory scrutiny. Any enforcement actions could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial position, and results of operations.

risk_heading: Risks Associated With Hazardous Air Pollutants From Maintenance Activities
paragraph_text:
Maintenance and turnaround activities at our facilities can temporarily increase emissions of hazardous air pollutants and particulate matter. During these periods, equipment may be opened, cleaned, repaired, or replaced, which can release fugitive contaminants from hoses, valves, ductwork, and storage containers. If contaminated waste is misclassified or improperly stored while awaiting disposal, it could increase enforcement and remediation risk.

Regulatory agencies may require additional monitoring and may impose stricter limits during operating periods identified as riskier. Citizen complaints or agency inquiries can also lead to sampling campaigns and unplanned operational constraints.

Our ability to successfully complete turnaround work without emissions incidents depends on contractor performance and timing. If we experience a release or significant emissions exceedance during maintenance, we could incur penalties, be required to implement costly corrective measures, and face operational delays that adversely affect our results.

risk_heading: Wastewater and Waste Handling Risks in Supply Chain Operations
paragraph_text:
In addition to our owned facilities, we rely on third-party suppliers that perform certain processing steps and manage scrap and waste generated from component production. While we impose contractual requirements regarding waste segregation, disposal methods, and documentation, the quality of suppliers’ waste handling can affect our compliance and liability exposure. If a supplier fails to properly manage waste streams—such as by draining process liquids into unauthorized systems or disposing of residues in non-permitted facilities—we could face adverse regulatory outcomes, requests for information, and potentially enforcement actions tied to our supply chain activities.

Supplier waste practices may also impact our ability to meet product-related compliance requirements, including limits on substances and requirements to document waste disposal pathways. For certain components, rejected material streams must be tracked to permitted processors. Incomplete documentation can lead to product shipment holds, increased costs, and delays.

Furthermore, suppliers may update processes or substitute raw materials without adequate notice, which can change the nature of waste streams and create misclassification risk. Audits and compliance checks can mitigate some risk but may not identify all issues, especially where suppliers handle waste informally or during peak production periods.

If we are unable to ensure that our suppliers manage waste and discharges in compliance with applicable requirements, our operations and financial results could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Risks of Releases of Wastewater and Contaminants
paragraph_text: We discharge treated wastewater and stormwater from industrial operations into managed water systems under applicable discharge permits. During periods of heavy rainfall, equipment maintenance, or process upsets, treatment systems may be unable to achieve permit limits, which could result in noncompliance or unauthorized discharges. The consequences may include enforcement actions, required corrective actions, increased monitoring and sampling costs, and the payment of administrative penalties. Certain constituents—such as nutrients, suspended solids, and trace metals—may be difficult to control consistently, particularly when feedstock quality varies or when new chemistries are introduced into our processes. In addition, our facilities rely on aging infrastructure, including pipelines, clarifiers, and retention basins, which may experience leaks or structural failures. If a release reaches groundwater or surrounding soils, we could face remediation obligations and potential claims from neighboring landowners or other affected parties. Even when releases are contained, the volume and duration of contamination may drive the cost and timing of remediation. These matters could adversely affect our operating performance and financial position.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Air Emissions from Industrial Processes
paragraph_text: Although we install pollution control equipment and monitor air emissions, our operations produce by-products and pollutants that are regulated under federal and state laws. Compliance may be challenged by process variability, abnormal operating conditions, and downtime of control devices, including baghouses, scrubbers, and thermal oxidizers. When these systems operate outside expected parameters, emissions could exceed permit limits, triggering enforcement, required reporting, and potential penalties. Some permits require continuous emission monitoring, and data quality issues may lead to findings of noncompliance. In addition, changes in emission standards or in the regulatory interpretation of existing standards could require additional capital expenditures and operational changes, such as redesigning processes or changing feedstock. If we cannot implement required controls within permitted timelines, our production could be curtailed or discontinued at affected sites. We may also be required to respond to community complaints or conduct investigations relating to odors, particulates, or other emissions. Any resulting remediation, settlement, or litigation could be costly and could divert management attention from operations. These factors could adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition.

risk_heading: Risks of Contamination at Former or Current Operating Sites

Environmental liabilities could have a material adverse effect on our financial condition.

Furthermore, if new requirements are implemented on short timelines, we may incur costs to temporarily store wastes until compliant treatment routes are available.

If regulators determine that we violated storage or manifesting requirements, they could impose penalties, require corrective action plans, or limit our ability to ship wastes. Litigation or citizen-suit claims may also be brought by third parties alleging improper waste management. Any such enforcement could increase costs and disrupt operations, which may negatively affect our results.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Our Workforce and Human Capital

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Health and Safety at Our Facilities
paragraph_text:
We operate facilities and maintain field operations where employees could be exposed to workplace hazards, including those related to industrial processes, vehicle operations, and maintenance activities. Although we maintain safety programs and policies and invest in training and protective equipment, workplace incidents can still occur due to human error, equipment failure, unforeseen operating conditions, or changes in staffing levels. Any significant accident, near-miss event, or regulatory inspection finding could result in work stoppages, increased insurance costs, remediation expenses, and reputational harm.

Our safety performance may also be affected by trends in labor availability. If we rely more heavily on temporary labor, contractors, or newly hired employees to meet production needs, the risk of incidents may increase because safety procedures and culture require time to learn and internalize. Additionally, evolving workplace regulations, including requirements related to ergonomics, respiratory protection, and incident reporting, may require changes to processes or staffing that increase costs.

In some circumstances, employees may refuse to work under certain conditions or may initiate work stoppages, which could impact customer deliveries. If we cannot prevent workplace injuries and comply with applicable health and safety requirements, our operating results and financial condition could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Labor Relations and Collective Bargaining

Even when we do not experience a work stoppage, negotiations may result in increased labor costs or changes to work rules that reduce operational flexibility.

In addition, we may face challenges in managing multiple bargaining units across regions and job classifications. Differences in contract terms, seniority rules, and wage structures may constrain our ability to reassign employees quickly in response to changing customer demand. These disruptions could impair our ability to meet contractual obligations, lead to liquidated damages or customer penalties, and negatively affect our financial results. We also could incur additional costs related to arbitration, legal proceedings, and workforce redeployment.

risk_heading: Risks of Employee Misconduct and Compliance Culture

Despite our training and oversight, misconduct by employees or contractors, including harassment, discrimination, retaliation, or violations of internal controls, could occur and may not be detected promptly. Inappropriate workplace behavior could lead to complaints, investigations, and potential employment-related claims or regulatory actions. Such matters could result in increased legal expenses, adverse judgments, and reputational harm that affects our ability to attract and retain employees.

Our risk is heightened by the scale and geographic distribution of our operations. Different local practices and varying levels of awareness of company policies can contribute to inconsistencies in implementation. If we fail to maintain a strong compliance culture, employees may engage in behavior that undermines trust and could result in operational errors.

In certain circumstances, we may need to take corrective actions, including removing individuals from critical roles, restructuring teams, or modifying training programs. These steps could be disruptive and may increase costs. Moreover, ongoing or future workforce investigations could divert management attention from operational priorities and negatively impact productivity.

While we seek to manage these risks through policies, ethics training, and reporting channels, we cannot assure that misconduct will not occur or that our processes will prevent or adequately address it.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Workforce Reductions and Restructuring
paragraph_text:
From time to time, we may undertake restructuring activities to align our cost structure with changing market conditions. Such actions may include reducing headcount, reorganizing departments, or outsourcing certain functions. Restructuring can create uncertainty for remaining employees and may negatively affect morale, retention, and productivity. In addition, the transition of responsibilities to new teams or vendors can introduce execution risk and increase the likelihood of errors.

Severance and other restructuring-related costs could increase if we are required to meet additional employment-related obligations under applicable laws, collective bargaining agreements, or contract terms. We also may experience unanticipated delays or constraints if labor authorities or works councils challenge aspects of workforce changes.

If we are not able to retain key personnel after restructuring, we could face gaps in critical knowledge and institutional experience. This could slow decision-making and reduce our ability to execute strategic initiatives, including technology upgrades and customer service improvements.

Further, workforce reductions may lead to a higher risk of workplace disputes, including wrongful termination or discrimination allegations. Even if we ultimately prevail, the process of defending claims could be costly and time-consuming and could divert management focus.

However, training effectiveness can vary across locations and over time, particularly as we onboard new employees, implement new systems, or introduce upgraded products.

If employees do not receive adequate training or training programs do not adequately cover changes in processes, we could experience increased defects, customer complaints, and returns. In addition, inadequate training may increase the likelihood of safety incidents and noncompliance with applicable workplace regulations. While we maintain quality management systems and internal audits, these controls cannot fully prevent errors.

We also face risk that training budgets may be reduced in response to cost pressures, or that employees may not complete required training in a timely manner due to staffing constraints. Such delays could lead to gaps in knowledge, especially for employees in critical roles.

Failure to maintain a sufficiently trained workforce could harm our ability to deliver high-quality products and services, and could result in greater expenses, lost revenue, and increased exposure to employment and regulatory matters.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Employee Retention and Knowledge Transfer
paragraph_text:
Our long-term success depends on maintaining experienced employees and ensuring effective knowledge transfer. As employees retire or transition to other opportunities, we may face challenges replacing their expertise, particularly for specialized manufacturing processes and customer-specific troubleshooting. In addition, organizations with significant use of institutional knowledge may experience reduced productivity if that knowledge is not captured and transmitted to newer employees.

To mitigate this risk, we implement succession planning and documentation practices. However, these measures may not fully prevent a loss of critical know-how. Knowledge transfer may fail if employees leave before completing handover, if documentation is incomplete, or if the new workforce lacks sufficient context to apply procedures correctly.

We may also experience increased attrition among high-performing employees if compensation adjustments do not keep pace with market rates, or if employees perceive limited career growth. Compensation and benefits are an important driver of retention, and increases in labor costs could negatively affect margins.

Any inability to retain experienced personnel and to transfer critical skills could adversely impact production continuity, customer support, and our ability to execute strategic projects, resulting in increased costs and reduced revenue.

risk_heading: Risks of Insufficient Staffing Levels and Shift Coverage

We also may face challenges in ensuring consistent training and compliance across multiple worksites and through third-party contractors.

risk_heading: Risks in Managing a Distributed Workforce During Public Health Events
paragraph_text:
We employ people across multiple geographic areas, with a portion of our workforce operating remotely and another portion working at client sites or in controlled environments. Public health events, including influenza outbreaks, pandemics, and related advisories, could result in illness, quarantines, travel restrictions, or reduced availability of employees. Even when disruptions are temporary, they can affect scheduling for project work, field services, and customer support.

We may need to modify business practices quickly, including shifting work arrangements, changing staffing levels, and increasing reliance on cross-trained employees. If we cannot maintain adequate staffing or if employees decline to travel due to health concerns, we could delay deliveries and incur incremental costs associated with overtime, temporary staffing, and remote coordination.

Public health events may also impact employee mental wellbeing and engagement, leading to increased turnover after a disruption. We may also face challenges ensuring that contractor personnel comply with relevant health and safety guidance. Any inability to respond effectively to public health disruptions could adversely affect our operations, customer relationships, and financial condition.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Use of Third-Party Contractors and Supply-Chain Labor Practices
paragraph_text:
A portion of our workforce is supported by contractors who perform operational and administrative activities, including logistics, warehousing, and certain specialized technical services. We may also depend on suppliers that employ large numbers of people to manufacture components or provide services. If these contractors or suppliers do not comply with applicable labor laws, wage requirements, working time restrictions, or workplace health and safety standards, our operations may be disrupted and our reputation may be harmed.

We conduct assessments and require contractual commitments related to labor standards, including expectations regarding freely chosen employment and appropriate working conditions. However, verifying compliance across multi-tier supply chains can be challenging, and identified noncompliance may not be remediated quickly. A supplier labor issue, such as unlawful practices or workplace hazards, could lead to production delays, termination of supplier relationships, or increased costs as we qualify alternative sources.

In addition, contractor turnover or staffing shortages can negatively affect quality, customer satisfaction, and continuity of service. If we fail to manage contractor performance and training, we may experience operational errors, employee disputes, or increased claims related to workplace conditions.

Any of these events could adversely affect our ability to meet customer demand and could result in significant financial and reputational impacts.
