Updates may inadvertently introduce defects, alter user workflows, or create unintended interactions with customer configurations. In addition, depending on customer environments, updates may cause system instability, incorrect outputs, or degraded user experiences. Although we use staged rollouts and regression testing, defects can still be discovered after wide deployment, particularly when customers operate products under conditions not covered by our testing.

If defects occur, we may need to suspend releases, provide emergency patches, or revert to prior versions. Such actions can be costly, may require additional support resources, and could negatively affect customer satisfaction. In severe cases, customers could allege that we negligently released defective software or that the software was not fit for its intended purpose, leading to claims for damages.

We also may face contractual consequences, including service-level credits and indemnification obligations, if our software fails to meet agreed performance parameters. Any significant remediation effort or litigation could have an adverse impact on our results of operations.

The risk of product harm from software regression increases as our products and integrations become more complex.

risk_heading: Supply Chain and Component Substitution Affecting Product Integrity

Even when alternatives meet functional specifications, differences in materials, tolerances, or calibration requirements can affect product integrity and performance. If alternative components fail earlier than expected or do not perform consistently, our products could malfunction and cause downstream impacts.

In addition to warranty and service costs, component-related issues may prompt customer complaints, returns, and recall actions. We could also face liability claims if a component substitution is alleged to have caused injury, property damage, or other harm. Resolving these matters could include reworking production, replacing parts, and providing remediation to customers.

To mitigate these risks, we conduct qualification testing and ongoing supplier monitoring, but these efforts may not capture all failure modes. Supplier test data may also be incomplete or inconsistent. Further, quality management systems at suppliers may not be aligned with our requirements.

A significant component quality incident could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

risk_heading: Risks from Defective Power Systems in Consumer Equipment

Certain of our consumer equipment products incorporate power supplies, batteries, and charging circuitry that operate under varying temperatures and usage patterns. Defective power-management design, manufacturing defects, or improper charging behavior can increase the risk of overheating, fires, or electric shock. While we apply safety testing and incorporate protective features, the inherent variability of consumer usage may result in conditions that exceed design tolerances.

If a safety incident occurs, we may be obligated to issue recalls, provide replacement equipment, and reimburse retailers for costs. We could also face liability claims from consumers, including allegations that we failed to design adequately or provide sufficient warnings and instructions. These claims may involve medical expenses, property damage, and alleged breach of implied warranties.

Regulators may investigate safety compliance and require changes to labels, packaging, or design. We may have to incur additional costs to improve thermal controls and to extend testing on new production lots.

Even a small number of incidents could result in significant reputational harm and reduced demand. We cannot assure you that our safety measures will prevent product-related injuries or that any resulting claims will not materially adversely affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Financial and Legal Exposure from Alleged Infringement in Product Functionality

Even where we believe claims are without merit, litigation can be costly and distracting. Our insurance may not cover all forms of infringement allegations, and any uncovered costs could adversely affect our financial results.

To reduce this risk, we maintain review processes for third-party licenses and technology use, and we monitor the product landscape. However, these measures cannot assure that disputes will not arise or that outcomes will be favorable.

An increase in legal actions related to product functionality could reduce demand and increase expenses, which could materially affect our business.

risk_heading: Potential Liability for Data Loss and Business Disruption from System Failures
paragraph_text:
Our products can be used to store, process, and manage information for customers. If our systems experience outages, data corruption, or defects that result in deletion of customer data, customers may suffer business interruption and operational losses. Such failures may occur due to software defects, infrastructure problems, configuration errors, or incorrect handling of backups and recovery processes. In some instances, third parties that provide supporting services may experience interruptions that affect the performance of our products.

Customers may seek remedies under service-level agreements and may pursue claims for breach of contract, negligence, or breach of warranty if they believe our product did not operate as represented. If a disruption affects consumers or regulated entities, additional claims may arise under consumer protection and data protection laws.

We can incur significant costs to restore service, recover data, and implement corrective measures to prevent recurrence. If interruptions are prolonged or occur repeatedly, customers may reduce usage, terminate subscriptions, or require greater indemnification.

Although we have business continuity and disaster recovery processes, these measures cannot ensure that data will always be accurate or recoverable in all circumstances. Any significant system failure or adverse outcome in legal proceedings could materially adversely affect our business, revenue, and reputation.

In addition, regulatory standards and scientific understanding may evolve. Because our products can be used in safety-critical applications, small performance variations may be alleged to have caused injury or property damage. Any such allegations, regardless of merit, could harm our brand and increase litigation expenses. A significant safety event could materially affect our business, results of operations, and financial condition.

risk_heading: Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks Associated with Our Connected Services

These offerings are subject to cyber attacks, ransomware, phishing, and other unauthorized access attempts. A security incident affecting our systems or the systems of third-party vendors could result in the loss or improper disclosure of sensitive information, disruption of service, and the need to notify affected individuals and regulators. Unauthorized access could also enable manipulation of device configurations or service behavior, which may impact product performance and create downstream safety and consumer-protection concerns.

We implement security controls intended to prevent or mitigate vulnerabilities, but we cannot ensure they will be effective against increasingly sophisticated threats. Our incident response processes may not adequately limit the scope, duration, or consequences of an attack. In addition, some threats may not be detected promptly, which could increase the harm to customers and require additional remediation costs.

If we fail to protect personal data or connected-service functionality, we may face contractual claims, regulatory investigations, enforcement actions, and lawsuits by end users. Such outcomes could materially and adversely affect our reputation and financial results.

risk_heading: Contamination and Defect Risks in Food and Beverage Ingredients

If contamination occurs, whether due to supply-chain issues, manufacturing deviations, or inadequate sanitation, we could face customer claims, withdrawal of products from shelves, regulatory inspections and enforcement, and recalls. Even where contamination is later determined not to be attributable to us, the reputational impact and associated legal and logistics costs could be significant.

We maintain quality systems and perform testing intended to detect contaminants, including microbial organisms and foreign material. However, not all hazards can be eliminated through testing, and the effectiveness of controls can be reduced by changes in supplier performance, new raw-material sources, or unexpected equipment failures. Additionally, some incidents may take time to surface, especially when contamination results in symptoms appearing after consumption.

If any of our ingredients are implicated in illnesses or adverse health effects, we could be named in product liability lawsuits and may be required to provide indemnities or other financial remedies. A major food safety event could materially harm our business by reducing demand, increasing costs, and restricting our ability to obtain new customers or contracts.

risk_heading: Failure to Meet Customer Service-Level Commitments for APIs
paragraph_text:
Some of our products are delivered as application programming interfaces (APIs) that customers use to build and operate consumer-facing applications. If we experience outages, incorrect responses, or corrupted data outputs, customers may be unable to complete transactions or may deliver erroneous information to end users. In addition, if our APIs fail to properly authenticate requests, there is a risk that unauthorized parties could exploit access to customer systems or data, leading to consumer harm.

We attempt to maintain service availability and data integrity through monitoring, redundancy, and testing. Nevertheless, failures can occur due to unforeseen technical issues, malicious activity, or changes in integrations performed by customers. When problems occur, we may be required to provide service credits, reimburse customers, or implement corrective actions quickly to prevent further harm.

Customers may interpret repeated failures as a breach of warranty or contractual service terms and could seek damages, including for losses suffered by their end users. In certain circumstances, end users may allege that our product caused misleading content, incorrect pricing, or privacy-related harm. Regulatory agencies may also request information if API failures affect consumers.

Because these products are used in real time, even short-lived issues can lead to claims and reputational damage. Any significant service disruption or security-related incident could materially adversely affect our business and results of operations.

risk_heading: Inadequate Sterility and Manufacturing Controls for Laboratory Supplies
paragraph_text:
We supply laboratory instruments and consumables used in research, medical testing, and manufacturing quality assurance. If our consumables are not sufficiently sterile, are contaminated, or fail to perform consistently, it could affect test results and customer operations. Depending on the customer’s use case, inaccurate outcomes could lead to delays in product development, incorrect laboratory conclusions, patient misdiagnosis allegations, or regulatory concerns for downstream parties.

Our manufacturing and packaging processes include sterilization steps, environmental monitoring, and lot-level release testing. However, sterility assurance is statistical and may not prevent every instance of contamination. Increases in production volume, changes in suppliers of single-use components, or unexpected equipment performance could reduce the effectiveness of controls.

If contaminated products are discovered, we could face customer claims, expedited shipping and revalidation costs, and potential recalls of affected lots. Claims could be brought under product liability theories or as breach of warranty and negligence. Additionally, if we are required to suspend shipments during investigations, we may incur significant lost revenue and additional compliance expenses.

We also may be required to respond to inspections by regulatory bodies and to enhance our quality systems. Any material failure in our ability to assure product quality could materially affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Failure to Adequately Protect Against Unauthorized Use of Customer Credentials
paragraph_text:
We provide workforce and security solutions that require customer credential management. If our systems do not properly enforce access controls or if we contain vulnerabilities that allow unauthorized access, attackers could compromise customer accounts and use our platform to access systems or data. Such misuse can directly relate to product functionality and could cause financial losses, data integrity issues, and operational disruptions for customers.

We invest in security engineering and implement authentication safeguards, logging, and anomaly detection. Despite these measures, it is possible that vulnerabilities could exist, that patches may be delayed, or that a breach could occur due to compromised credentials provided by customers or sophisticated social engineering. A breach may also involve our third-party service providers, whose controls could be insufficient to prevent unauthorized access.

If we are unable to prevent unauthorized use, we could face claims from customers alleging negligent security practices, breach of contract, breach of warranty, or violations of applicable laws related to consumer and end-user protection. Regulators may also seek to impose remediation requirements and penalties. In addition, we may be required to offer enhancements or refunds to affected customers, and we could incur significant expenses to investigate incidents and improve security.

Any such outcomes could harm our reputation and have a material adverse effect on our financial position and results of operations.

risk_heading: Potential Liability for Misleading Safety Communications and Product Warnings
paragraph_text:
Our products include user instructions, safety signage, and digital guidance intended to inform customers about safe installation and use. If the information we provide is inaccurate, incomplete, or not updated to reflect known risks, we could be exposed to claims alleging failure to warn or breach of consumer protection laws. Plaintiffs may argue that our warnings did not adequately address foreseeable misuse, installation errors by third parties, or changes in operating conditions after purchase.

In addition, we may need to update product documentation as new information becomes available, including findings from field experience, internal testing, or regulator communications. If customers do not receive updates promptly, or if updates are not incorporated into digitally delivered materials, we may face increased risk of harm and subsequent litigation.

We also rely on retailers and service providers to distribute materials and to assist customers with installation and maintenance. If those third parties provide incorrect guidance or fail to follow our specifications, customers may still seek damages from us, and we could bear a portion of the settlement or defense costs.

A significant adverse event involving personal injury, property damage, or substantial economic loss could lead to settlements, increased warranty accruals, and substantial legal expenses. Accordingly, liability related to safety communications and warnings could have a material impact on our results of operations.

risk_heading: Product Performance Failures in Autonomous and Assisted Features
paragraph_text:
We design components and software used in vehicles and related mobility equipment that may include driver-assistance and automated features. If our technology performs incorrectly due to sensor calibration issues, software logic errors, or insufficient verification across varied weather and road conditions, the outcomes could include vehicle malfunctions, collisions, or other safety incidents. Even where responsibility may be shared among multiple system providers, customers and injured parties frequently name multiple participants in product liability actions.

Our development processes incorporate simulations, data-driven validations, and field testing. However, autonomous and assisted systems operate in complex, unpredictable environments, and testing may not fully account for all condition permutations. Updates made via over-the-air software revisions can also introduce regressions or unexpected interactions with customer-installed configurations.

If an incident is alleged to involve our components or software, we could be subject to recalls, regulatory investigations, and lawsuits. Recall campaigns can be costly, may require coordination with manufacturers and service centers, and could reduce sales while remediation is completed. Regulatory agencies may impose additional reporting and testing requirements that could delay future deployments.

Claims could also include allegations that our products failed to disclose limitations or safety risks adequately. Any material adverse outcome could harm our reputation and result in significant expense and loss of revenue.

risk_heading: Risks of Intellectual Property Claims Tied to Product Design Defects
paragraph_text:
We face a risk of product-related litigation not only for safety and performance, but also for alleged infringement or misuse of third-party technology included in our products. If a claim asserts that a component, algorithm, or user interface infringes intellectual property rights, we may be forced to modify or redesign features. Those changes could require re-validation, potentially delaying product releases and increasing costs. In certain cases, modification efforts may inadvertently introduce defects or performance issues, which could then result in additional warranty obligations or consumer protection disputes.

Because products are distributed through multiple channels, customers may experience changes in functionality that differ from their expectations. If those customers argue that our redesigns reduce safety, reliability, or usability, they may pursue claims for breach of warranty or for damages arising from product malfunction.

Even when we believe we have strong defenses, the expense of defending intellectual property claims and related injunctive relief can be substantial. Adverse outcomes could restrict our ability to sell products and may also require customer remediation, refunds, or recalls if safety-related features must be altered.

While these matters primarily involve intellectual property, they can quickly translate into product liability and consumer protection exposure when design changes affect how products perform.

Accordingly, litigation related to product design and technology could materially affect our business.

risk_heading: Risks of Misallocation of Charges and Billing System Errors Causing Customer Harm
paragraph_text:
We provide payments-related products used by merchants to collect consumer payments and generate receipts. While our contracts typically limit certain liabilities, errors in transaction processing—such as incorrect charge amounts, duplicate captures, improper refunds, or misapplied taxes—could harm customers and merchants. Such failures can occur due to defects in payment processing software, configuration mistakes, or malfunctions in integrations with card networks and banking partners.

Our systems are designed with reconciliation tools and monitoring; however, monitoring may not detect all issues quickly, especially during peak transaction periods or when external payment rails change. In addition, changes in our product features or merchant-specific configurations may increase the risk of edge-case errors.

If customers or consumers assert that our products caused financial loss, delayed processing, or unauthorized charges, we may face chargeback costs, indemnification obligations, and lawsuits alleging breach of warranty, negligence, or consumer protection violations. Regulatory agencies may also investigate if public disclosures about charge processing are alleged to be misleading or if customers experience repeated payment errors.

Even where outcomes are ultimately resolved in our favor, the associated legal and remediation costs could be material. A significant increase in claims or regulatory actions could adversely affect our reputation and operating results.

risk_heading: Quality Variability in Replacement Parts and Aftermarket Compatibility
paragraph_text:
Our aftermarket replacement parts are installed by service centers and independent mechanics into older equipment. Compatibility and quality are critical because a part that does not fit properly or does not perform within specification may lead to equipment damage, safety risks, and customer downtime. If any portion of our replacement parts are defective, improperly manufactured, or inconsistently calibrated across production lots, we may face returns, warranty claims, and claims asserting product malfunction.

We attempt to design parts to match widely used specifications and maintain documentation to guide correct installation. Nonetheless, because installation practices vary and some customers may use parts in nonstandard configurations, real-world performance may differ from expectations. In addition, suppliers may introduce changes in manufacturing processes, coatings, or materials without timely notice.

If customers believe a part caused damage or injury, they may pursue product liability claims or seek indemnification under service contracts. Even if we do not admit liability, the costs of investigation, recalls of affected SKUs, and legal defenses may be substantial. Recalls can also strain relationships with retailers and increase inventory and distribution costs.

Accordingly, quality variability or aftermarket compatibility issues could materially affect our revenue and profitability.

risk_heading: Risks of Adverse Outcomes from Software Updates and Automatic Feature Activation
paragraph_text:
We periodically release software updates for our products, including security patches and new functionality. Some updates may change system behavior, data handling methods, or user workflows. While our release process includes validation and phased rollouts, updates can still contain defects, create performance degradation, or inadvertently enable features without adequate user consent. If an update causes a product to perform incorrectly—such as producing erroneous outputs, failing to enforce access restrictions, or disrupting integrations—customers may suffer business interruption and end users may be impacted.

If the affected customers are unable to correct the issue quickly, they may pursue claims for breach of warranty, negligence, or damages related to product malfunction. Under certain privacy and consumer protection frameworks, an alleged failure to provide required notice or obtain appropriate permissions may result in regulatory action and civil penalties.

We may also be required to roll back updates, provide compensatory credits, or release emergency patches. These activities can strain engineering resources and may increase the likelihood of additional issues.

Even where we believe the impact will be limited, a widely deployed update can affect a large installed base simultaneously. As a result, software update-related failures could have a disproportionately adverse effect on our revenue and costs, including potential litigation and remediation expenses.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Recurring Defects in Critical Safety Systems
paragraph_text:
Certain of our products incorporate safety-critical systems designed to protect users and property. If these systems fail to detect hazards, activate protective mechanisms when required, or otherwise function within prescribed tolerances, customers could be exposed to injury or property damage. Safety-critical defects may also result in mandatory reporting and corrective actions to regulators, as well as customer-requested retrofits.

We depend on multiple layers of inspection and verification, including functional tests and review of component certifications. However, safety systems can be complex, and failures may result from subtle interactions among software logic, sensors, and power electronics. Additionally, component aging, varying environmental conditions, and changes in supplier manufacturing processes could cause performance drift over time.

A pattern of recurring defects could lead to increased warranty costs and greater risk of class actions brought by customers alleging that our products were not reasonably safe. Plaintiffs may assert negligence, breach of warranty, and failure to warn, and may demand damages related to injuries, property damage, and related economic losses.

Even if we are able to successfully remediate defects, the reputational harm and administrative burden associated with investigations, audits, and corrective campaigns could materially affect our sales and operating margins.

While we maintain product liability insurance, coverage may be limited, and our insurers may dispute claims. Any material recall, regulatory action, or litigation could adversely affect our results of operations and financial position.

In addition, claims for personal injury or other damages may be asserted, and our insurance coverage may be insufficient to cover all liabilities. Any failure to maintain compliance with applicable medical device regulations, including post-market surveillance obligations, could also materially harm our business and results of operations.

If we are required to issue notices, revise specifications, or conduct broad replacement programs, our reputation and customer relationships could be harmed, and our results of operations could be adversely affected.

In addition to financial losses and increased security and legal costs, any incident could damage our brand and reduce customer willingness to adopt our products. If vulnerabilities are discovered by third parties or regulators before we have implemented mitigations, the resulting public attention and litigation could materially affect our business.

In addition, we may face allegations that we failed to provide adequate warnings or that our packaging design did not anticipate realistic distribution risks.

If a product incident occurs, plaintiffs may argue that a failure to warn or instruct was a contributing factor to injuries or losses. We support community programs through direct giving, employee volunteerism, and in-kind contributions. These activities are intended to enhance social outcomes in communities where we operate, including education initiatives, workforce development, and relief efforts during local emergencies. While we evaluate such programs to align with our values and applicable laws, our community investment commitments can become subject to public scrutiny if outcomes are disputed, if beneficiaries raise concerns regarding fairness or access, or if stakeholders question whether contributions are sufficient relative to the impacts of our operations.

Additionally, our ability to provide grants and related services may be affected by economic conditions, changes in tax rules, and the availability of qualified community partners. If our partners experience governance issues, misallocation of funds, or compliance failures, we may face reputational harm and, in some circumstances, legal exposure. We also rely on local nonprofit and school administrators to coordinate logistics and tracking of outcomes; deficiencies in reporting can create uncertainty regarding the effectiveness of our initiatives.

We may be required to restructure or discontinue programs in response to stakeholder feedback or regulatory requirements. Such changes could adversely affect our relationships with community leaders and may hinder our broader ability to secure support for future projects.

risk_heading: Community Opposition to Transportation and Access Changes
paragraph_text:
We operate a network of logistics assets and rely on road and rail transportation to supply products to customers. From time to time, we may pursue route optimization, changes to staging areas, or new distribution hubs to improve efficiency. These changes can affect neighborhood traffic patterns and access to local services, particularly in areas adjacent to freight corridors and intermodal yards. Community groups may object on the grounds that increased deliveries will heighten congestion, increase noise, or make it harder for residents to access schools, healthcare facilities, and public transit.

If community opposition intensifies, we may face additional permitting requirements, conditions on delivery hours, or restrictions on certain routes. Local authorities may also require infrastructure improvements, such as roadway upgrades, pedestrian crossings, and additional signage. While we work with agencies to plan for safety and community needs, implementation of such measures can increase costs and delay schedule changes.

In certain jurisdictions, public comment periods and local elections may introduce uncertainty about whether previously approved plans remain acceptable. If we are unable to maintain alignment with community expectations and local decision-makers, the benefits of logistics optimization may not be realized within expected timeframes, and operations may experience disruptions.

risk_heading: Risks of Social Tension Related to Local Economic Impacts
paragraph_text:
We may contribute to local employment and commerce, but our presence can also create local economic imbalances, particularly during periods of rapid expansion or contraction. For example, increased demand for housing, construction labor, and local services can strain affordability and availability in the communities where we operate. If residents view these changes as displacing long-term inhabitants or increasing cost of living, social tensions may rise and community sentiment can affect our ability to operate.

These tensions can surface as organized opposition to land use changes, demands for local hiring quotas, or pressure to provide additional community benefits. Authorities may consider new requirements for procurement from local vendors or for community benefit agreements as a condition of approvals. While such arrangements can support local outcomes, they can also increase costs, create administrative burdens, and constrain our supply-chain flexibility.

If we fail to communicate clearly about expected workforce needs, purchasing practices, and timelines for project milestones, community concerns may grow. Additionally, if economic conditions deteriorate due to factors unrelated to us, residents may attribute hardships to our operations. Such dynamics can amplify protests, disrupt site access, and increase risk of operational interruptions.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Operating in Regions with Weak Community Infrastructure
paragraph_text:
In certain locations, community infrastructure such as roads, healthcare access, and emergency response capacity may be limited or uneven. During periods of peak activity—such as major construction phases, seasonal demand surges, or severe weather—local systems may be unable to keep pace with increased traffic and service needs. While we coordinate with local authorities, our ability to reduce impacts depends on the availability and responsiveness of external parties.

If local emergency services cannot effectively respond to incidents involving our workforce, contractors, or visitors, we may be required to implement additional preparedness measures, including funding or supplying specialized equipment, training local responders, and enhancing on-site capabilities. These measures can require significant capital expenditures and may not fully substitute for gaps in local infrastructure.

In communities where access to communications is limited, our ability to disseminate timely notices about planned disruptions, evacuation guidance, or safety information may be constrained. Incorrect or delayed communications can heighten community frustration and increase the risk of misinformation spreading.

If we are unable to maintain effective coordination with local officials and community organizations, we could face delayed approvals, operational stoppages, or increased claims by community members relating to perceived harms.

risk_heading: Regulatory and Community Impacts from Changes to Local Service Plans
paragraph_text:
We may implement changes to local service models, including customer service locations, delivery schedules, and community-facing support programs. These changes are intended to improve efficiency and accessibility; however, communities—especially those with limited internet access or limited transportation options—may have difficulty transitioning to new arrangements. If residents experience reduced availability of assistance or believe that we are not serving all segments of the community fairly, community organizations may file complaints to regulators or request investigations.

Our customer service and field operations also depend on public-facing events, such as town halls and neighborhood outreach sessions. If stakeholders perceive these forums as not addressing concerns, our engagement could be criticized in media reports and social networks, leading to reputational harm. Increased scrutiny may lead to additional requirements for multilingual communications, extended hours, or additional physical sites.

Additionally, our ability to manage community relations can be affected by local leadership turnover. New city officials or council members may revisit prior understandings about operational practices, delivery routes, and community benefit agreements. Where prior commitments are not well-documented or rely on informal relationships, we may need to renegotiate terms, which could delay implementation.

If these factors result in disruptions to local service access or heightened regulatory involvement, our financial results and growth plans could be adversely impacted.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Stakeholder Expectations for Local Hiring and Workforce Development
paragraph_text:
We are subject to community expectations and, in some jurisdictions, contractual commitments regarding local hiring, apprenticeship opportunities, and workforce development. While these programs can strengthen community ties, they can also create operational constraints. Changes in local labor market conditions, shortages of qualified candidates, and competition from other employers may limit our ability to meet hiring targets on time. When communities perceive unmet commitments as unfair—particularly in disadvantaged areas—stakeholder pressure can increase.

We also provide training initiatives intended to prepare local residents for available roles. If training capacity is insufficient, or if participating candidates do not achieve expected competencies despite reasonable support, community leaders may question program effectiveness. In addition, employee turnover among trainers and partner organizations can disrupt program continuity. These factors could lead to disputes with community organizations or additional requirements from regulators and contracting authorities.

If we are required to expand training programs beyond planned budgets, or to offer extended guarantees of employment, our operating costs could rise. Moreover, any misalignment between community expectations and actual operational needs may harm our reputation and adversely affect the approval process for future expansions and facility modifications.

risk_heading: Potential Community Impact and Disputes from Land Use and Access Rights
paragraph_text:
Our projects may require changes to land use, access rights, or easements. These activities can impact local residents, including through changes in walking routes, access to private property, or restrictions on temporary use of community areas. Even when we obtain legal rights, stakeholders may contest the fairness of compensation, the sufficiency of alternative access, or the timing of construction-related relocations.

Disputes can involve claims by landowners, community organizations, and local government officials, including allegations that our representatives did not adequately consult affected parties. Such disputes can delay construction and increase costs for mediation, legal proceedings, or additional engineering to redesign access points. If disputes are escalated through political channels, local officials may condition approvals on renewed consultation.

We also depend on rights-of-way controlled by third parties, such as municipalities and transportation authorities. If those parties renegotiate access conditions or publicize concerns regarding community impacts, we may face operational limitations or additional capital expenditures.

Failure to manage land use-related community impacts could lead to work stoppages, adverse publicity, and longer permitting timelines, which could affect our ability to execute development plans.

risk_heading: Risks from Community Health and Wellbeing Concerns Following Local Incidents
paragraph_text:
From time to time, we may experience incidents involving our facilities, operations, or deliveries that result in community questions about health and wellbeing. While we maintain safety procedures and investigate incidents, community concerns may extend beyond the specific event and may be amplified by misinformation. In communities where residents rely on local health providers and public information channels, delays in communication or overly technical explanations can contribute to heightened anxiety.

When we determine that an incident requires community notification or support, we may need to provide expanded guidance, establish hotlines, and fund temporary assistance programs. If community expectations exceed what we can reasonably provide, or if our remediation or support measures are not perceived as equitable, community members may file claims, seek regulatory action, or organize protests.

We also engage with community advisory groups in certain locations to discuss operational updates and incident learnings. If advisory group members become dissatisfied, withdraw support, or receive information from parties with competing narratives, trust can be reduced and engagement may become less effective.

Any failure to respond appropriately to community health and wellbeing concerns, including those affecting vulnerable populations, could result in operational constraints, increased litigation and claim expenses, and long-term reputational damage.

risk_heading: Community Benefit Agreement Challenges and Public Scrutiny
paragraph_text:
In connection with certain development projects, we may enter into community benefit agreements or similar arrangements with local entities. These agreements can include commitments such as funding for neighborhood improvements, support for local education programs, and measures intended to address community concerns. If communities disagree on the prioritization of benefits, on governance of funds, or on reporting transparency, public scrutiny may increase.

Community benefit arrangements can also be affected by changes in local leadership, shifting political priorities, and differing views on whether benefits were delivered as promised. Where agreements rely on third-party organizations to administer funds, governance weaknesses or underperformance by those organizations may create reputational harm to us, even if we have exercised oversight reasonably.

If we cannot meet timelines for benefit delivery due to delays in project schedules, procurement constraints, or administrative disputes, stakeholders may demand renegotiation or seek remedies. Additionally, community leaders may use broader political narratives to frame our agreements as insufficient, which can attract media attention and protests.

Such outcomes could restrict our ability to obtain approvals for future phases, increase compliance and reporting obligations, and lead to higher costs. Failure to sustain constructive relationships with community stakeholders could adversely affect our operational and financial performance.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Engagement and Consent Requirements in Certain Jurisdictions
paragraph_text:
In some jurisdictions and for certain project types, we may face requirements relating to community engagement, public consent, or consultation with affected groups. While these processes are designed to ensure that stakeholders understand the planned activities and potential impacts, the timing and scope of engagement can vary. If consultations are challenged on procedural grounds, or if stakeholders claim that important groups were excluded, authorities may suspend or delay approvals.

We also rely on community representatives to communicate information and gather feedback. Miscommunication can occur when representatives provide incomplete information, or when community members interpret technical materials differently. In addition, community engagement processes can be disrupted by periods of civic unrest, local labor disputes, or security conditions. Where engagement meetings cannot proceed as planned, we may be required to repeat consultation activities, which increases costs and extends schedules.

Our ability to maintain community trust may further depend on perceived fairness in how impacts are distributed. If affected residents believe that benefits accrue to others while burdens remain local, the support necessary to proceed with projects may decline.

If we are unable to secure and sustain constructive community engagement and obtain required approvals in a timely manner, our ability to develop projects and achieve planned returns could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Potential Community Disruptions from Utility Interconnections and Construction Activities
paragraph_text:
Certain projects require new utility interconnections and related construction work, which can disrupt community access to services and create neighborhood inconvenience. Utility outages, temporary service interruptions, or pressure/flow fluctuations in affected areas—even if brief and localized—may generate public complaints and calls to local officials. Residents may also experience short-term interruptions to essential services and may require assistance locating temporary alternatives.

When we plan work, we coordinate with utility operators and municipalities. However, outages may be affected by circumstances outside our control, including contractor performance issues, equipment availability, and unexpected conditions encountered during installation. If service disruptions occur more frequently or for longer periods than communicated, community trust can be damaged and political pressure can intensify.

We may be asked to provide additional notice periods, expand call-center availability, reimburse certain costs for affected residents, or fund improvements to neighborhood infrastructure. Such actions can increase operating costs and can also create administrative burdens for documentation and dispute resolution.

In some areas, community organizations may request that communications be provided in multiple languages and accessible formats. Failure to meet these expectations could increase reputational risk and trigger complaints to regulators.

Any substantial disruption to community services or ineffective communication could adversely affect project timelines and our ability to maintain social license to operate.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Community Feedback on Construction Noise, Dust, and Scheduling
paragraph_text:
During construction and maintenance activities, we may generate noise, dust, and traffic changes that affect residents near our sites. Although we implement controls designed to reduce nuisances, community feedback may lead to additional operating limitations. Local residents may request earlier scheduling changes, expanded work-hour restrictions, or additional community notification. Where neighborhoods are densely populated or include sensitive facilities, such as schools or community centers, the tolerance for temporary disruption may be lower.

Community complaints can also influence city or county enforcement actions. If authorities increase inspections or require additional documentation in response to frequent complaints, our projects may experience delays. Even where underlying issues are addressed, repeated nuisance allegations can create a perception of disregard for community wellbeing.

We seek to respond through mechanisms such as dedicated complaint hotlines and on-site representatives. However, community concerns may not be resolved promptly if staffing resources are limited, if complaints are submitted after work hours, or if the information provided by residents is incomplete. In addition, misalignment between our internal schedules and the expectations communicated to residents can exacerbate tensions.

If our ability to manage community nuisance concerns is insufficient, it could result in enforcement actions, litigation risk, and increased costs associated with mitigation measures and schedule adjustments.

risk_heading: Community Trust Risks Associated with Public Information and Transparency Practices
paragraph_text:
We provide information to communities about our operations, safety preparedness, and project updates through websites, public meetings, and written notices. Community trust can be undermined if residents believe that information is incomplete, inconsistent, or difficult to understand. Technical terminology, language barriers, or differences between our internal understanding and public messaging can lead to confusion.

Where communities include non-native speakers or persons without reliable access to digital resources, our outreach channels may not reach intended audiences. If residents do not receive effective notice regarding changes to schedules, transportation patterns, or temporary facility restrictions, they may attribute disruptions to negligence or concealment. This can lead to complaints, media inquiries, and requests for independent verification.

Additionally, community stakeholders may seek transparency regarding spending of community benefit funds, the selection of partner organizations, or the criteria used for local workforce opportunities. If our disclosures are delayed or perceived as overly promotional, stakeholders may challenge our practices and seek third-party audits.

We also depend on timely reporting from contractors and service providers. If contractors fail to communicate community impacts in accordance with contractual requirements, community sentiment may worsen and our ability to remediate concerns may be delayed.

If we cannot maintain clear, consistent, and accessible communication with communities, we may experience increased regulatory attention, reputational harm, and challenges obtaining approvals for future activities.

risk_heading: Financial Strain on Community Programs and Resulting Stakeholder Disputes
paragraph_text:
We may co-fund community programs that support local services, such as childcare initiatives, educational partnerships, and emergency relief resources, often through multi-year agreements with community-based organizations. These programs typically involve budgeted contributions and defined performance indicators. If our financial results decline, capital constraints, or changes in operating plans reduce our expected contributions, we may face difficult decisions regarding scaling back or deferring program obligations.

Even where reductions are consistent with our contractual or legal rights, community stakeholders may perceive the changes as reneging on commitments. Such perceptions can lead to disputes, negative media coverage, and requests for intervention by local government entities that originally facilitated partnerships. Additionally, if community organizations rely on our funding to maintain staffing and service capacity, they may be compelled to reduce services, which can exacerbate community hardship and intensify scrutiny of our role.

There is also risk that performance indicators may be subject to interpretation by different stakeholders. If program outcomes are delayed due to factors outside our control, such as local enrollment challenges or partner staffing limitations, the parties may disagree about whether objectives were met.

These disputes can increase legal and administrative costs, consume management attention, and damage our relationships with community organizations. Adverse outcomes could impair our ability to secure future partnership opportunities.

risk_heading: Risk of Social Unrest and Disruptions in Communities Where We Operate
paragraph_text:

In certain geographies, economic stressors, public-health challenges, or political conditions can lead to social unrest, protests, or labor disturbances. Community tensions may be intensified by perceived inequality in economic benefits, concerns about safety, or disruptions caused by construction and operational activities.

When demonstrations or civil disturbances occur, our employees may face challenges commuting, securing housing, or obtaining medical assistance, and our vendors may experience delays in delivering goods and services. Increased security measures could divert resources and reduce operational efficiency. In extreme cases, authorities may impose curfews or temporary closures that interrupt production and shipping.

We attempt to maintain open lines of communication with local leaders and community organizations, including outreach and grievance mechanisms. However, if community expectations are not met, if information about our activities is inaccurate or misrepresented, or if we do not respond in a timely manner, community relations may deteriorate. Any prolonged disruption to community stability, even without a direct operational failure, could adversely affect our results of operations and cash flows.

If permitting timelines extend materially due to community input, objections, or required modifications, we could incur higher costs and experience disruptions that negatively affect our ability to execute our capital plan and maintain reliable service to our customers.

Any delay or disruption could reduce our ability to meet customer demand and could result in additional expenses related to mitigation measures, security, and dispute resolution. These risks may adversely affect our financial performance.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Shareholder Activism and Changes in Corporate Strategy
paragraph_text:

From time to time, stockholders may propose changes to board composition, executive compensation, governance provisions, or operational priorities. Proxy contests and settlements can divert management attention and resources from our operating and risk management priorities. Even when we ultimately prevail, activism can create uncertainty in our relationships with customers, partners, and lenders, and can lead to short-term decision-making pressures that may not reflect long-term value creation. Additionally, if stockholders pursue proposals that require amendments to our charter or bylaws, we may be exposed to litigation or regulatory scrutiny. In extreme cases, such activities could disrupt our ability to execute financing plans or complete transactions within expected timeframes.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Major Decisions Under Stockholder Consent Requirements
paragraph_text:

The timing and outcome of any approvals may be influenced by investor perceptions of our performance, macroeconomic conditions, or governance practices. If approvals are delayed or denied, we may be unable to pursue opportunities, refinance obligations, or restructure certain liabilities on favorable terms.

Even where the approvals are obtained, dissenting stockholders could assert claims challenging the adequacy of disclosures made in connection with requested votes, or allege that fiduciary duties were not satisfied. These claims may result in litigation costs, potential injunctive relief that delays corporate action, or settlements that reduce value. Our governance structure includes committees and voting procedures intended to mitigate these risks; however, these measures cannot eliminate the possibility of regulatory investigations or private actions arising from contested decisions.

risk_heading: Risks of Ineffective Governance of Information and Regulatory Disclosures
paragraph_text:
We rely on information systems and internal governance processes to prepare and review regulatory filings, including quarterly and annual reports. Our disclosure governance includes controls over who may access material nonpublic information, how employees escalate concerns, and how drafts are reviewed by finance, legal, and executive leadership. If these processes are not followed, if there are communication breakdowns between functions, or if systems do not capture updated information in a timely manner, we could disclose incomplete or inaccurate information.

Regulators may request additional documentation or initiate investigations if filings are later found to contain material errors, even if unintentional. In addition, governance failures related to classification of risks and commitments could lead to misstatements in our narrative disclosures, which may result in restatements, enforcement actions, or shareholder lawsuits. The risk of disclosure problems increases when we integrate new businesses, implement new enterprise software, or operate across multiple jurisdictions with differing reporting requirements.

We maintain policies and training programs intended to reduce these risks, but there can be no assurance that our governance and controls will prevent all errors or miscommunications.

risk_heading: Risks Related to the Independence of Our Audit Committee
paragraph_text:
Our audit committee is responsible for overseeing the integrity of our financial statements and the independent audit process. The committee’s oversight includes reviewing the scope of audit work, monitoring independence and performance of our independent registered public accounting firm, and considering the adequacy of internal control. If the audit committee lacks independence or sufficient expertise, or if it cannot access timely information from management, its ability to challenge assumptions and evaluate judgments may be limited.

In addition, audit fee levels, non-audit services, and reliance on certain personnel may affect perceptions of audit independence. While we seek to comply with applicable rules, changes in accounting standards and heightened regulatory scrutiny can increase the complexity of audit planning and the judgment required from both management and auditors. If the audit committee does not effectively manage these matters, it may contribute to the risk of misstatement or incomplete disclosures.

Any issues identified by our auditors or audit committee—whether in internal control testing or substantive audit procedures—could require management to take corrective actions. Such actions may be costly and may consume significant time from leadership and finance personnel.

risk_heading: Risks from Conflicts of Interest in Related-Party Transactions
paragraph_text:
We enter into transactions with customers, suppliers, and other counterparties that may have relationships with members of our Board or executive officers or their affiliates. Although we maintain policies intended to identify, review, and approve related-party transactions, conflicts of interest can arise and may not always be fully mitigated. A related-party transaction could be structured in a manner that provides less favorable terms than those available from unrelated parties, or could involve greater business risk, particularly when counterparties influence procurement decisions.

If any related-party transaction is challenged by stockholders or regulators, we may face litigation, demands for additional disclosures, or delays in receiving approvals required under our governance policies. Even if a transaction is ultimately approved, perceived conflicts may harm our reputation and affect investor confidence. Governance procedures, such as committee review and document retention, are designed to provide transparency; however, they may not prevent disagreements about fairness or independence.

We could also be required to unwind or renegotiate transactions if a counterparty’s financial condition deteriorates or if counterparties fail to comply with contractual or regulatory requirements.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Merger and Acquisition Governance Decisions
paragraph_text:
Strategic acquisitions and investments require significant governance decisions by management and our Board. These decisions include evaluating financial due diligence, approving consideration structures, determining whether to pursue indemnities, and establishing post-closing oversight responsibilities. If our due diligence is incomplete or if the governance process does not appropriately weigh key risks, we may acquire businesses that expose us to unexpected liabilities, including those related to product quality systems, regulatory compliance, or customer contracts.

Our internal governance also determines integration milestones and authority levels for sign-off on material changes to financial controls, vendor arrangements, and key contracts. If authority is unclear or if integration is managed through insufficient oversight, employees may deviate from approved policies. In addition, governance changes may be required to comply with new securities regulations or exchange listing requirements after an acquisition.

Even where integration proceeds as planned, stockholders may disagree with acquisition rationale or governance outcomes and could initiate legal proceedings related to disclosure or process. Such actions can be disruptive and may divert resources from integration work.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Delegation of Authority and Management Accountability
paragraph_text:
Our risk management and operating controls are supported by a delegation-of-authority framework that defines approval thresholds for spending, contracting, and changes to critical business processes. If delegation is too broad, employees may enter into commitments without sufficient review, increasing the likelihood of documentation errors, mispricing, or contractual noncompliance. Conversely, if delegation is too narrow, operational delays could cause missed opportunities and may lead to exceptions that bypass approved procedures.

We rely on management accountability mechanisms—including periodic attestations, compliance reporting, and escalation to executive leadership—to confirm that approvals are executed properly. If personnel misunderstand authority limits, if training is inadequate, or if reporting channels fail, governance controls may not operate as intended. In certain circumstances, such failures could result in inaccurate recognition of liabilities, disputes with counterparties, or regulatory issues.

Additionally, our internal reporting system depends on the timely submission of information by business owners. If those submissions are late or incomplete, governance bodies may rely on outdated information when assessing materiality and making disclosure decisions. This could negatively affect both investor perception and our ability to respond quickly to emerging risks.

risk_heading: Risks from Governance-Related Software and Data Access Controls
paragraph_text:
As part of our enterprise risk controls, we implement access restrictions and approval workflows for sensitive data, including information used in financial close, contract administration, and regulatory submissions. Governance over information technology includes the segregation of duties between system administrators, reporting personnel, and approvers. If access privileges are not updated promptly after personnel changes, if role-based controls are misconfigured, or if approval workflows are circumvented, unauthorized changes could occur to financial systems, reporting tools, or record repositories.

Although these matters often intersect with cybersecurity, our risk relates primarily to the governance of authority and approvals within our systems. Unauthorized or improper changes could lead to errors in reported results, delayed filings, or difficulties in substantiating financial data to auditors and regulators. Moreover, governance gaps in change management could affect the reliability of automated reporting processes.

We regularly review user access and system changes, but there can be no assurance that our controls will detect or prevent every unauthorized action. Any resulting remediation efforts could be significant and could also require enhancements to board oversight and audit committee reporting.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Material Judgments and Governance of Accounting Estimates
paragraph_text:
A substantial portion of our financial results depends on management’s judgments and estimates, including those related to impairment testing, valuation of deferred tax assets, allowances for credit losses, and assessment of contingencies. Our governance process for these estimates includes periodic review by senior finance leaders, corroboration from subject matter experts, and escalation to the audit committee for significant matters. If those processes are not followed consistently or if estimates are based on incomplete data, the risk of misstatement increases.

Our internal governance also governs how we document assumptions and how we communicate changes in methodology. If policy changes are implemented without adequate review or if there is insufficient documentation, our disclosures could be challenged. Additionally, when new accounting standards become effective, even well-designed governance processes may require interpretation and training that can temporarily increase the likelihood of error.

While we seek to maintain robust oversight, there can be no assurance that our controls and governance procedures will prevent all errors or that auditors and regulators will agree with our conclusions. Any significant adjustment to our estimates could require restatement of prior periods and could adversely affect our results and stock price.

Our oversight relies on reporting packages, periodic meetings, and controls testing at the subsidiary level. Our whistleblower program is subject to change as governance best practices and regulatory requirements evolve. However, there is no guarantee that our reporting and investigation processes will always operate as intended or that the outcomes will satisfy all parties involved.

risk_heading: Risks Related to the Composition and Qualification of Key Executives
paragraph_text:
Our strategy depends on the leadership and judgment of our executive team and, in particular, on the continuity of key executives who oversee finance, operations, and risk management. Corporate governance arrangements, including succession planning and committee oversight, are intended to reduce the operational disruption that can occur when senior leaders depart unexpectedly. However, there can be no assurance that succession plans will identify suitable replacements in a timely manner or that new executives will quickly adapt to our control environment.

If a key executive leaves, the Board may rely on interim leadership while conducting searches. Interim arrangements could create gaps in oversight of internal controls, management reporting, and budget execution. In addition, changes in leadership may lead to revisions in governance priorities, reporting cadence, and approval thresholds, which could temporarily weaken control effectiveness.

Investors and proxy advisors may also evaluate governance based on executive transitions and board responsiveness. Negative perceptions could lead to increased activism or reduced support for management proposals. Any resulting uncertainty could affect our ability to complete capital markets transactions or to negotiate financing terms.

We attempt to maintain strong governance practices; nonetheless, leadership turnover is outside our control and could have adverse effects on our operating performance and disclosure obligations.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Compliance with Departmental Sign-Off Requirements for Grants and Commitments
paragraph_text:
We approve certain corporate commitments—such as customer-facing sponsorship arrangements, grants to nonprofit entities, and commitments to marketing campaigns—through internal governance procedures requiring departmental review and executive sign-off. These requirements are intended to ensure that commitments are consistent with corporate policies, properly documented, and appropriately disclosed when material. If internal sign-off requirements are not followed due to turnover, unclear responsibilities, or system workflow errors, we could enter into commitments that create reputational risk or require disclosure beyond initial expectations.

Our governance process also considers whether counterparties are subject to compliance checks, including screening for sanctions or politically exposed persons where applicable. While our compliance team performs periodic reviews, governance reliance on departmental attestations may lead to gaps if attestations are not sufficiently supported by documentation. If later investigations identify that a counterparty should have been screened more thoroughly, we may be required to suspend payments, unwind arrangements, or remediate disclosure records.

Any failure to follow governance sign-off and documentation practices could result in regulatory scrutiny, shareholder complaints, and costly corrective actions. Even where the underlying business judgment is sound, procedural failures in governance can trigger adverse outcomes.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Governance of Risk Appetite, Approvals, and Materiality Thresholds
paragraph_text:
We maintain a risk governance framework that sets our risk appetite, defines materiality thresholds, and establishes escalation and approval processes for transactions and initiatives that could affect our financial condition. The framework is overseen by management committees and reviewed periodically by the Board. If the risk appetite framework is outdated, if assumptions about market conditions prove incorrect, or if thresholds are not updated to reflect changes in strategy, we may approve activities that carry risks beyond what the company is positioned to manage.

Governance also governs how we define “material” events for internal escalation, which influences timing and content of disclosures. If personnel interpret thresholds inconsistently or fail to escalate issues promptly, governance bodies may make decisions without timely information. Conversely, overly conservative thresholds could slow decisions and reduce the company’s ability to respond competitively.

We use reporting to monitor compliance with governance requirements, but reporting quality depends on the completeness and accuracy of inputs from business units. Inadequate data can impair risk committees’ ability to assess exposures, including those related to contract performance and counterparties’ obligations. Any resulting governance failures could lead to losses, restatements, or regulatory actions.

risk_heading: Risks Associated With Board Oversight and Internal Controls
paragraph_text:
Our ability to prevent and detect material misstatements in our financial statements depends on the effectiveness of our disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting. These controls are designed to provide reasonable assurance, but they cannot guarantee that errors, omissions, fraud, or management override will not occur. As we grow, restructure, or expand into new markets, we may introduce new systems, reporting processes, and personnel, which can increase the risk of control failures. In addition, changes in accounting standards, regulatory requirements, and auditing practices may require enhancements to our controls that take time to implement and validate.

If we identify material weaknesses or significant deficiencies in our internal controls, we may be required to restate financial results or incur additional costs to remediate control deficiencies. Any such event could adversely affect investor confidence, our ability to obtain financing on favorable terms, and our compliance with securities laws. Further, even when deficiencies are remediated, the remediation efforts may not prevent future occurrences, particularly in periods of rapid operational change or cost pressures.

risk_heading: Risk of Conflicts and Limitations in Related-Party Transactions
paragraph_text:
We enter into transactions with affiliates and other parties with which certain of our directors, executive officers, or significant investors may have relationships. While we attempt to evaluate such transactions through appropriate governance procedures, including committee review and approval where required, these processes may not eliminate all conflicts of interest or ensure that terms are as favorable as those that would be available in purely arm’s-length negotiations. Related-party arrangements may also change over time as ownership structures, management incentives, or strategic priorities evolve.

If any of these transactions are challenged by regulators, investors, or under applicable corporate law, we could face adverse outcomes, including penalties, rescission of agreements, or increased litigation and administrative costs. In addition, conflicts of interest may impair decision-making and create reputational harm, which could negatively affect our relationships with customers, business partners, and capital providers. Even absent wrongdoing, the existence of related-party relationships can subject us to heightened scrutiny and could result in delays in executing transactions needed for our business.

risk_heading: Shareholder Voting Risks From Concentrated Ownership
paragraph_text:
A significant portion of our voting power is held by a limited number of stockholders and their affiliates. As a result, these holders may be able to influence the outcome of matters submitted to our shareholders, including the election of directors, approval of certain amendments to our charter, and approval of major corporate transactions. This concentrated ownership may reduce the likelihood of other shareholders influencing governance outcomes, even if they disagree with the controlling holders’ positions.

From time to time, differences in strategy between major stockholders and the broader investor base may lead to prolonged proxy contests, negotiated settlements, or litigation challenging governance actions. These events can consume management time and resources and may create uncertainty regarding our long-term strategy. Moreover, provisions in our governing documents, together with applicable Delaware and federal law, may make it harder for minority stockholders to pursue governance reforms or to replace directors.

Any inability to reach consensus among shareholders could adversely affect our access to capital, market perception, and our ability to execute business plans. These dynamics could also affect the timing and terms of potential acquisitions or other transactions we pursue.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Executive Compensation and Incentive Alignment

The selection and calibration of performance metrics can be complex, and metrics may not fully capture the risks associated with business decisions, including timing, regulatory outcomes, or market volatility. If our compensation outcomes are perceived as misaligned with performance, investors may withhold support for executive compensation proposals or directors.

In addition, changes in governance policies, accounting rules, and proxy advisory expectations could require modifications to our compensation practices. These changes may reduce the effectiveness of our incentive arrangements or increase costs associated with administration, disclosure, and compliance. If we are unable to attract and retain qualified executives due to perceived governance or compensation concerns, our operating results could suffer.

Board committees oversee elements of compensation, yet committee determinations are subject to judgment and information available at the time. Material events occurring after metrics are set may not be reflected in compensation calculations. These factors could result in reputational damage and increased costs, including potential litigation or administrative inquiries related to compensation disclosure and governance practices.

risk_heading: Limitations on Dividend Payments and Shareholder Return
paragraph_text:
We may not pay dividends at any particular time or in amounts that stockholders expect. The declaration and payment of dividends are subject to the discretion of our board of directors and depend on a variety of factors, including our financial performance, restrictions under debt agreements, regulatory considerations, and our capital needs. Even if we generate sufficient earnings, we may retain cash to fund operations, investments, or strategic opportunities.

If our board determines that paying dividends is not prudent, dividends could be reduced, suspended, or eliminated. Dividend policy can also affect investor demand, which may influence our stock price and overall market valuation. In addition, any repurchase of shares, if authorized, could require the board to balance capital allocation against liquidity needs and covenants. Changes in interest rates, economic conditions, and credit availability may further constrain our ability to return capital.

Stockholders should not rely on dividends as a source of return. Any failure to meet dividend expectations could result in negative market reaction, heightened volatility, and reduced liquidity for our common stock.

risk_heading: Risks From Changes in Auditors and Audit Committee Oversight
paragraph_text:
Our audit committee oversees the appointment, compensation, and retention of our independent registered public accounting firm, and it evaluates performance and independence. However, the audit committee’s oversight may be challenged, and auditors may resign or be replaced for reasons that may be disruptive to our reporting cycle. Changes in audit firms can lead to differing audit approaches, timelines, and interpretations of critical accounting policies.

If auditor independence is called into question or if we cannot obtain timely audit services, we could face delays in filing periodic reports and potential noncompliance with listing standards. In addition, changes in audit personnel may affect the continuity of audit work and increase the risk that issues are identified later than expected. These factors could require additional audit procedures, which would increase costs and could also affect management’s ability to focus on operations.

Any restatement or material adjustment following an audit could adversely affect our credibility with investors and regulators. Weaknesses in audit planning or communication between management, the audit committee, and auditors can also impair our financial reporting and increase the likelihood of future control issues.

risk_heading: Joint Venture Governance and Deadlock Risks
paragraph_text:
We participate in joint ventures and strategic arrangements with other companies that may share ownership, decision-making authority, and economic interests. Under these structures, significant actions often require approval of the venture’s governing bodies, which may include consent rights for each party or voting thresholds that do not align with our interests. Disagreements regarding strategy, capital expenditures, personnel, or accounting policies can result in delayed decisions or governance deadlock.

If we are unable to resolve disputes with our partners, we may be required to accept unfavorable outcomes, such as reduced control over operational decisions or changes in the allocation of resources. Deadlock may also cause the venture to suspend projects, miss deadlines, or incur additional costs related to dispute resolution. In some cases, our contractual rights may be insufficient to compel our partners to perform or to provide us with information necessary to manage the risks of the arrangement.

These governance issues can adversely affect our ability to realize the expected benefits of the joint venture and may increase our exposure to reputational harm and litigation. Even when a dispute is ultimately resolved, the time and expense required can reduce profitability and impair long-term value creation.

risk_heading: Failure to Comply With Listing and Corporate Governance Requirements

We must comply with the corporate governance rules of the national securities exchange and with applicable SEC requirements, including those related to audit committee composition, internal governance policies, and timely periodic filings. If our board or committees do not meet the requirements of the exchange for any reason, or if we fail to maintain appropriate disclosure controls and procedures, we could become subject to notices of noncompliance or delisting risk.

For example, changes in committee membership due to resignations, vacancies, or regulatory interpretations may temporarily impact compliance. Additionally, new or amended rules could require updates to our governance charters, committee responsibilities, and disclosure processes. Implementing these changes may require time and could increase the risk of procedural mistakes.

Noncompliance with listing standards could also result in increased scrutiny by regulators, investors, and proxy advisory firms, which may affect our stock price and cost of capital. If we are required to delay filings to address compliance issues, we could incur penalties and face investor concerns regarding our governance and reporting reliability.

While we invest in corporate governance and compliance infrastructure, no system can fully prevent errors, and any governance-related deficiency could have material adverse effects on our business and financial condition.

risk_heading: Uncertainty Regarding Board and Committee Composition
